Discrimination diagrams based on Au-As/Sb and Se/Ge-Co/Ni demonstrate that gold precipitation was controlled by multiple coupled processes, including fluid-rock reaction, fluid boiling, and meteoric water mixing, which collectively destabilized Au(HS)2 - complexes and triggered gold deposition. EBSD results show that Tudui pyrites primarily experienced brittle deformation with subordinate plastic deformation, creating extensive microstructures and crystal defects that acted as favorable sites for gold deposition. These microstructures also established preferential pathways for trace element diffusion, enabling Au and other elements to migrate and precipitate along microfractures driven by chemical gradients between pyrite cores and rims. Overall, the Tudui deposit represents a structurally controlled, coupled metallogenic system. This study establishes an integrated macro-micro-scale model for mineralization in Jiaodong-type deposits and provides a theoretical basis for regional gold exploration in the Jiaodong Peninsula.

title: Photo-stimulated reductive dissolved Fe 2+ from epitaxial twinned goethite accelerated by fulvic acid: Insight from the band structure and photochemical activity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Shanshan Yang, Fei Liu, Xiao Ge, Hongrui Ding, Anhuai Lu
abstract: The photo-stimulated reductive dissolution of semiconducting iron (hydro)oxides plays a vital role in iron (bio)geochemistry processes. Epitaxial twinned goethite (Goe-Hem), a typical goethite twin composed of a hematite center with acicular goethite outgrowths, is widely distributed in natural environment. Nevertheless, studies exploring the photochemical activity of Goe-Hem remain limited. In this study, photo-stimulated reductive dissolution process of Goe-Hem were investigated in depth. Physicochemical characterization revealed that Goe-Hem consists of twinned goethite crystals with a hematite core, containing 73% goethite and 27% hematite. In the presence of fulvic acid, the concentration of photo-stimulated reductively dissolved Fe2+ (aq) from Goe-Hem was higher than that from goethite. Consequently, Goe-Hem exhibited superior photo-stimulated reductive ability than goethite. This enhanced activity was ascribed to the stronger visible light absorption, narrower band gap energy and more negative conduction band energy of Goe-Hem relative to goethite. The photo-stimulated reductively dissolved Fe2+ (aq) from Goe-Hem play a vital role in iron cycling and biological iron acquisition in nature.

title: Human activities as primary drivers of marine and inland groundwater salinization in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Christian Narvaez-Montoya, Saugata Datta, Jürgen Mahlknecht, Miguel Rangel-Medina
abstract: Groundwater salinization is a major threat to coastal aquifers worldwide, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions subjected to intensive groundwater use. Understanding the behavior of individual coastal aquifer systems is therefore essential to support effective groundwater management. This study evaluates the spatiotemporal salinization patterns of the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system, located at the coastal margin of the Sonoran Desert, using 357 groundwater samples collected in 2009 and 2016, primarily from the most productive and shallow hydrogeological unit. Multivariate and hydrogeochemical analyses suggest that seawater intrusion is the dominant driver of total dissolved solids and chloride enrichment, strongly linked to long-term overexploitation. Inland, heterogeneous nitrate and sulfate distributions suggest the influence of anthropogenic inputs, including urban wastewater infiltration and irrigation return flow. Temporal comparisons indicate a decrease in nitrate concentrations, likely reflecting improved wastewater treatment, alongside a significant increase in sulfate, which may be associated with enhanced water-rock interaction processes previously linked to irrigation practices. 15% of samples exceed drinking water guideline limits, and 47% exhibit poor irrigation water quality, highlighting potential risks for human consumption, soil salinization, and agricultural productivity. This study provides one of the most comprehensive recent assessments of salinization processes in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system and emphasizes the need to reduce groundwater abstraction and strengthen wastewater and irrigation management to prevent further degradation of the aquifer. Because the interpretations are based on major ions and previous studies, future investigations incorporating more sensitive tracers are needed to better constrain the mechanisms responsible for groundwater salinization.

title: Geochemical fractionation, mineralogical insights and environmental risk of toxic elements in mining-impacted soils of Zamfara State, Nigeria
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Jajati Mandal, Waheed Ariyo Bakare, Effiom Oku, Barnabas Iliya Musa, Abhishek Sharma, A.S.M. Fazle Bari, Michael D. Wood, Simon M. Hutchinson, Debapriya Mondal, Mohammad Mahmudur Rahman
abstract: This study examined the concentrations, geochemical partitioning, mineralogical controls, and probable mobility of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in mining impacted surface soils from Anka, Zamfara State, Nigeria. Soil samples (n = 50) were analyzed for physicochemical properties, total elemental burdens, and sequential extraction fractions. The soils ranged from sandy loam to clay loam and showed moderately acidic to near-neutral pH, elevated organic carbon, and high cation exchange capacity, reflecting substantial capacity for metal retention. Total elemental concentrations revealed lead (Pb) in the highest amount (1240.23 ± 92.94 mg kg−1), compared to arsenic (As), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), barium (Ba), and iron (Fe). Correlation studies indicated strong associations between Ba-Fe and Mn-Pb, suggesting shared mineralogical or oxide-based controls on distribution. Sequential extraction revealed marked differences in elemental mobility. Lead was primarily bound to reducible Fe-Mn oxides (∼83%), with only ∼13% in the extractable fraction. Arsenic was dominated by residual and oxidizable pools (>90%), indicating minimal mobility. However, Ba and Fe remained primarily in residual and reducible forms. In contrast, Zn was highly labile, with nearly 90% occurring in the extractable fraction displaying mixed extractable and reducible associations and reflecting its redox sensitivity. Mineralogical analyses confirmed quartz-dominant soils containing illite, muscovite, albite, galena, and Pb-As jarosite, with SEM-EDS further verifying PbS (galena), supporting the limited bioavailability of Pb in oxic conditions. Risk Assessment Code (RAC) values placed As in low-risk and Fe in the no-risk category, Ba in medium to high risk, Mn in high risk and Pb in medium risk, and Zn in very high risk (∼90%). Overall ecological risk ranking followed the order Zn > Mn > Ba > Pb > As > Fe. These findings highlight that while total Pb remains elevated, its mobility is restricted by mineralogical sinks, whereas Zn, despite low concentrations, exhibits high mobility and environmental responsiveness. These contrasting behaviours emphasize the need to interpret total elemental concentrations alongside geochemical fractionation when assessing contamination risk in mining-impacted landscapes.

title: Stable isotope fingerprints of Ni-Cu-PGE sulfide remobilization in Mesoarchean ultramafic-mafic rocks
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Shounak Dutta, Sisir K. Mondal
abstract: The origin of enigmatic Archean breccia-hosted Ni-Cu-PGE deposits is often debated because primary orthomagmatic and secondary hydrothermal mineralization can be difficult to distinguish. In this study, we investigate the Mesoarchean Nuasahi Ultramafic-Mafic Complex (India) using integrated petrology, mineral chemistry, and S-O-H isotope geochemistry to resolve the history of metal mobilization in its breccia zone. Our results data reveal a multi-stage mineralization process. An initial magmatic stage involved the interaction of a fluid-rich gabbroic melt with ultramafic-chromitite clasts, which induced sulfide liquid immiscibility and formed a high-temperature (∼950 °C) pyrrhotite–pentlandite–chalcopyrite assemblage with a mantle-like sulfur isotope composition (δ34S ∼ 0‰). The primary assemblage was later overprinted by hydrothermal alteration, characterised by the replacement of chromite by ferrianchromite and the growth of secondary pyrite-chalcopyrite at a lower temperature. Secondary chalcopyrite is selectively enriched in 34S (δ34S ∼ 1‰) relative to the primary pyrrhotite, producing pronounced isotopic disequilibrium. Oxygen and hydrogen isotopes in coexisting chlorite (δ18O ∼2.4‰; δD ∼ −28‰) indicate that the altering fluid resembled heated Archean seawater. We propose that the infiltration of this seawater remobilized primary sulfides, concentrating mobile chalcophile elements such as Pd. At the same time, the overall mantle-like sulfur signature was retained due to the low sulfate content of the Archean oceans. Selective sulfur-isotope disequilibrium in sulfide pairs thus provides a robust tracer of cryptic seawater-driven hydrothermal remobilization in ancient ultramafic-hosted ore systems.

title: Mineralogical and geochemical controls on Co-V-Pt-Ni enrichment in manganese mineralization: evidence from the Dilli deposit, Eastern Türkiye
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Mehmet Ali Gücer, Okay Çimen, Alican Aktağ, Serdar Keskin
abstract: The growing demand for critical minerals driven by the global energy transition and advanced technologies highlights the importance of unconventional metal reservoirs. This study investigates the Ni-, Co-, V-, and Pt-enriched Dilli manganese deposit (Kemaliye-Erzincan, Eastern Türkiye) to constrain the mineralogical, geochemical, and genetic controls on critical metal enrichment in Mn oxide mineralization. An integrated approach combining field observations, petrography, X-ray diffraction (XRD), whole-rock geochemistry, mineral chemistry, and stable C-O isotope analysis was applied to better understand the potential origin of critical mineral enrichments. The mineralization is dominated by Mn4+-bearing oxides, principally pyrolusite and hollandite, accompanied by minor rhodochrosite. High MnO (39-64 wt%) and very low Al2O3 and Fe2O3 contents indicate chemical precipitation with negligible detrital input. Discrimination diagrams and trace-element systematics consistently support a structurally controlled hydrothermal origin. Chondrite-normalized REE patterns display low total REE and very low Nd contents comparable to typical hydrothermal deposits, whereas neutral to slightly positive Ce anomalies and non-chondritic Y/Ho ratios suggest limited oxidative interaction with surface-derived fluids rather than primary marine hydrogenetic growth. Stable C–O isotope compositions of co-genetic calcite are inconsistent with a purely marine depositional environment and indicate precipitation from low-to moderate-temperature hydrothermal fluids. Mineral chemistry reveals strong phase-specific partitioning: hollandite preferentially incorporates V and Ba, whereas pyrolusite is enriched in Ni. Cobalt occurs in both phases, whereas Pt may also be present in both Mn oxide phases, suggesting that trace-element distribution is influenced by both crystallochemical and physicochemical controls. The enrichment of Ni, Co, and Pt is most plausibly linked to hydrothermal fluid circulation through ultramafic units, which likely acted as the primary metal source prior to precipitation. The Dilli deposit thus represents a structurally controlled hydrothermal Mn system enriched in critical metals, emphasizing the exploration relevance of Mn oxide mineral chemistry in identifying alternative sources of critical metals in Türkiye.

title: Relative kinetics of precipitation of barium chromate and barite in groundwater
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Abhas Singh, Mainak Bhattacharya, Ashwini Kumar Mohapatra
abstract: Water-soluble and carcinogenic hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] poses serious health risks due to its potential migration in aquifers and interaction with naturally present barium [Ba] to form sparingly soluble colloidal barium chromate [BaCrO4(s)]. However, Ba may also react with other solutes predominantly present in many groundwaters like dissolved sulfate [SO4], causing precipitation of barite [BaSO4(s)]. The eventual fate of Cr(VI) in such groundwaters may be governed by the relative rates of formation of these two solids, which are currently not known. In this contribution, simultaneous formation of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) in groundwater matrix and their relative kinetics were investigated through continuous flow stirred tank reactor experiments. Chromium-free Ba-spiked SO4-containing groundwater was introduced into the reactor, preloaded with Ba-free Cr(VI)-spiked SO4-containing groundwater, at a flow rate of 0.2 mL min−1. Aqueous samples were collected with time and analyzed for Cr(VI), SO4, Ba, and pH till steady-state was attained. Geochemical analysis of solute data and characterization of the precipitated solids confirmed rapid formation of a solid solution of ∼86 mol% BaCrO4(s) and ∼14 mol% BaSO4(s). Solution saturation indices with respect to BaCrO4(s) gradually decreased over time, but persistent supersaturation with BaSO4(s) suggested conditions favorable for formation of BaSO4(s). Time-dependent Cr(VI), SO4, and Ba concentrations were modelled with process-based mass balance equations. Optimized surface area normalized precipitation rate constants of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) were obtained as 6.3-8.6 × 10−8 mol m−2 s−1 and 1.3 × 10−8 mol m−2 s−1, respectively, indicating that BaCrO4(s) precipitates approximately five times faster than BaSO4(s). Determination of these constants would help in accurate prediction of Cr(VI) transport in contaminated aquifers rich in Ba and possibly similar co-solutes.

title: XAS evidence for Sb(V)-ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-magnetite during anoxic incubation of stormwater road basin sediments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Areej Adra, Maëva Philippe, Pierre Le Pape, Georges Ona-Nguema, Gautier Landrot, Ludovic Delbes, Elora Bourbon, Katell Quénéa, Sophie Ayrault
abstract: Antimony (Sb) presents versatile chemical forms in urban (sub)surface environments, the identity of which being driven by local redox conditions. Due to its use as additive in products for its flame-retardant properties, urban environments such as the Parisian area (Paris, France) are particularly subjected to Sb contamination. This is particularly observed in stormwater basin sediments, collecting Sb from runoff on road surfaces. Here, we used these sediments as a reactive ecosystem for aging Sb-bearing ferrihydrite, standing as a classical Sb carrier phase of surface environments and as possible input phase to the basins. Batch experiments were performed by mixing stormwater pond sediments plus Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite (Fh-Sb(V)) and were aged up to 210 days under a water column in oxic or anoxic conditions. For each series, an individual batch sample was sampled at 1, 7, 28 and 210 days of aging. Liquid samples were analyzed by ICP-MS, while Fe and Sb speciation were studied by X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES/EXAFS) to study Sb release to surface waters and the temporal evolution of Sb speciation. Whatever the experimental conditions, Sb release into solution remains below one percent of the initial stock introduced in the sediment, decorrelated of Fe(II) release and organic matter consumption during reduction processes. Under anoxic conditions, XANES data at the Fe K-edge show the transformation of ferrihydrite into magnetite. From EXAFS analysis at the Sb K-edge, we unambiguously identify a novel reaction route, Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-bearing magnetite, likely resulting from anoxic aging in a biotic medium. In the oxic experiment, diffusion of air through the initially anoxic water column resulted in the late oxidation of the newly Sb(III)-magnetite formed into Sb(V)-bearing phases. This study shows the strong geochemical reactivity of Sb when submitted to redox fluctuations and that iron-reducing activity likely drives Sb speciation in the presence of available Fe from poorly-crystalline ferrihydrite (Fh). Thus, the fundamental knowledge we bring here could help to define conditions propitious to limiting soluble Sb release from the solid phase in contaminated sediments submitted to redox fluctuations.

title: Uranium remobilization from a riparian wetland: Implications on long-term stewardship and extreme rain events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Daniel I. Kaplan, Karah M. Greene, Wei Xing, Arelis M. Rivera-Giboyeaux, Kenneth M. Kemner, Peng Lin
abstract: Natural attenuation of contaminants by wetlands can cause them to become secondary sources of contamination. The objectives of this field study were to: 1) measure the remobilization of uranium (U) in a stream flowing through a contaminated wetland in South Carolina, USA, and 2) develop empirical relationships between rainfall and U remobilization. Stream water was sampled hourly during six storm events ranging from 0.69 to 9.87 cm of rainfall, which caused flow to increase by as much as 1100% with respect to base flow. Uranium concentrations in all filtered samples, U < 0.45μm, were below the Maximum Contaminant Limit of 30 μg/L U. Conversely, as much as 94 vol% of the U in stream samples (g U/L streamwater) was associated with suspended solids, U ≥ 0.45μm. Consequently, significant correlations (p < 0.01) existed between stream water total U and suspended solids concentrations (or turbidity). Using a linear relationship (p < 0.01) between rainfall and remobilized U (g-U/sampling-event), it was estimated that 29% of the remobilized U in the year 2024 occurred during the three days of greatest rainfall. Similarly, using historical rainfall data, it was estimated that 864 kg-U, or 2.2% of the original 43,500 kg-U released into the wetland 55 years ago had been remobilized. This value of remobilized U is consistent with U-mass balance at the study site. Predictions of increased regional total rainfall and the number of extreme rainfall events may increase the rate of contaminant dispersion from riparian systems.

title: Harmful gas generation potential and disaster mechanisms in coastal sediments of Shenzhen Bay, China: Insights from geochemical characteristics and depositional environment
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Yuxuan Liu, Peidong Su, Peng Qiu, Yougui Li, Jun Sasaki
abstract: The flammability and toxicity of harmful gases pose significant safety risks during underground engineering construction. However, theoretical frameworks for the early-stage investigation of the generation potential and hazard mechanisms of shallow biogenic gases in coastal zones remain insufficient. In this study, three underground construction areas in the coastal zone of Shenzhen Bay, China, were selected as the research sites. Integrated organic and inorganic geochemical analyses were applied to systematically reconstruct the depositional environmental characteristics of the tunnel construction areas, evaluate potential for biogenic harmful gas generation, and explore their potential disaster mechanisms. The results indicate that the sediments in the study area contain relatively high organic matter with mixed terrestrial and marine sources and remain at a low maturity stage, providing favorable conditions for biogenic gas generation. In the Pearl River Estuary-Qianhai Bay tunnel construction site, the positive relationship between (Mo/U)EF and total sulfur (TS) suggests weak but episodic sulfidic conditions at the construction depth, likely associated with stronger hydrodynamic activity and lower sedimentation rates that facilitate sulfate penetration, indicating a higher potential for combined CH4-H2S hazards. In contrast, the Deep Bay tunnel site is characterized by weak hydrodynamics, high sedimentation rates, and strongly reducing conditions. The weakly correlated relationship between (Mo/U)EF and TS indicates dominance of methanogenesis, suggesting a methane-dominated hazard potential. Finally, a conceptual investigation framework for biogenic harmful gases in coastal underground engineering is proposed to support early risk identification and prevention.

title: Differential responses of vanadate reduction to soil aggregate types
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Zhenhan Li, Song Wang, Fengyuan Zhuang, Qinghao Zhang, Baogang Zhang
abstract: Different soil aggregate fractions create distinct biogeochemical microhabitats, driving divergent ecological adaptations and functional traits. In this study, different aggregate fractions from a vanadium-contaminated soil were inoculated into the reactors to evaluate their differences in pentavalent vanadium [V(V)] reduction capacity. Micro-aggregates (MiA) achieved the highest V(V) removal efficiency of 96.2 ± 0.12% and the fastest first-order removal kinetics (rate constant 0.06 h−1), followed by medium aggregates, small aggregates, and large aggregates. The microbial consortia from aggregate could transform toxic soluble V(V) into less mobile tetravalent vanadium [V(IV)] precipitates, thereby contributing to the remediation of vanadium-contaminated soil. During the V(V) reduction process, microbial communities underwent significant changes, exhibiting lower richness and diversity and forming a distinct cluster compared to the initial samples. Meanwhile, the relative abundance of metal-reducing genera increased from 5.29 ± 0.79% to 39.2 ± 12.3%. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed tight microbial collaboration, whereas larger aggregate fractions were associated with lower V(V) removal efficiency. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that V(V) reduction genes were potentially associated with reductive metabolism and electron transfer genes. The microbiome in MiA exhibited the highest cytochrome c levels and the strongest expression of potential V(V) reduction genes of omcB and narG, highlighting microorganisms derived from MiA-aggregates as primary drivers of vanadium detoxification in contaminated soils.

title: Phase-specific particle size distributions in Hanford tank waste measured by automated SEM–EDS: A statistical comparison across a waste column
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Edgar C. Buck, Austin A. Bachman, Jarrod R. Allred, Carolyn A.M. Burns, Amy M. Westesen, Reid A. Peterson
abstract: This study supports in-tank sludge washing and delivery of initial feed to the Hanford High-Level Waste vitrification facility by characterizing particle populations in 241-AN-106 wastes from the southeast quadrant of the Hanford Site. We developed computational tools to determine particle size distributions for specific mineralogical phases within these heterogeneous sludges. Automated Particle Analysis (APA), combining scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), was used to quantify particle morphology and composition for tens of thousands of individual particles, providing phase-resolved particle size distributions that are more representative than manual measurements. Phase-specific size distributions were compared among positions within a series of 241-AN-106 core-samples, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic was applied to test for statistically significant differences. Results demonstrate measurable size separation of gibbsite particle populations with position within the sludge layers, where larger gibbsite particles partitioned to the lower segments. This study illustrates how high-throughput, phase-resolved particle sizing can improve understanding of waste heterogeneity relevant to washing and feed delivery.

title: The performance of PHREEQC databases for modelling the solubility of CO 2 , N 2 , CO 2 -N 2 mixtures, calcite and barite at elevated temperatures, pressures and electrolyte concentrations
description: Publication date: Available online 11 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Knud Dideriksen, Hanne Dahl Holmslykke, Bi Yun Zhen-Wu, Jakob Molander, Claus Kjøller
abstract: Modelling of geochemical reactions in the deeper subsurface can provide valuable insight into the state and dynamics of a system where processes are complicated to observe. In addition, it allows prediction of the outcome of interventions, such as geothermal exploitation or CO2 injection. The degree to which the modelling portrays reality depends in part on the ability of the thermodynamic data to describe solubility of gases and solids accurately. For most modelling software, the thermodynamic data is typically compiled in databases, which have been tested to some extent. However, the capabilities of the databases to accurately calculate solubility over a wide range of conditions are most often not well defined. This study tests the performance of 13 PHREEQC databases, benchmarking them against an empirical dataset with 3147 measurements of the solubility of CO2(g), N2(g), CO2(g) - N2(g) mixtures, calcite, and barite at variable temperature, pressure, and electrolyte concentration. Our work shows that the databases employing the Peng-Robinson equation of state and molar volume changes of reaction are generally capable of correctly describing experimental values of solubility at higher pressure as intended. Databases relying on the Pitzer approach for description of activity coefficients often provide reasonably accurate calculations of solubility at an extended range of electrolyte concentrations at variable temperature and pressure. For many databases, including those based on Pitzer equations, calculations substantially deviate from measured values at conditions that are unexpected based on general expectations to database performance. This is particularly true for simulations of calcite solubility. Identifying these deviations requires tests such as the one given here. Our approach allows selection of databases based on the objective criterion that calculations should match empirical data at or near the modelled conditions as closely as possible. We exemplify the use of our results for database selection for the simulation of calcite scaling in a model geothermal well. To enable users and developers of databases to conduct tests of performance themselves, the supplementary information contains experimental data, input files and Python code for calculations.

title: Precipitation dominance in regulating the carbonate weathering carbon sink flux: Insights from a regionally calibrated GEM-CO 2 model
description: Publication date: Available online 11 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Yuxia Hou, Fen Huang, Huan Liu, Chencong Li, Tongbin Zhu, Jianhua Cao, Qiong Xiao, Pei Wang, Bill Hu
abstract: Reliance on global parameterization impedes the accurate quantification of carbonate weathering carbon sink flux (CCSF), injecting significant uncertainty into regional carbon budgets. To resolve this, we developed a regionally calibrated GEM-CO2 model (CGEM-CO2 model) for the karst region of Guangxi, China. Constrained by local hydrochemical data, the CGEM-CO2 model yielded a calibrated parameter of 1.6313, achieving a robust fit with observations (R2 = 0.8459). Validation at the point scale confirmed that the calibrated model outperforms both the original GEM-CO2 and Maximal Potential Dissolution (MPD) models, particularly in resolving spatial heterogeneity. The model estimates a mean CCSF of 9.18 t C km-2 yr-1 for 2000–2022, revealing a distinct “V-shaped” temporal trend characterized by an initial decline and a post-2011 recovery, concentrated in northern Guangxi. Concurrently, a steady rise in equilibrium HCO3 - concentrations indicates an intensifying carbon sink potential, likely driven by soil CO2 enrichment. Geospatial analyses identified a “precipitation-dominant, multi-factor synergistic” mechanism driving the CCSF’s spatial variability. Precipitation was identified as the primary positive driver, with its explanatory power significantly amplified through interactions with factors such as evapotranspiration and NDVI. These findings demonstrate that regional model calibration is critical for refining carbon budget assessments and elucidating the complex interplay of climatic and ecological drivers. This approach provides a robust framework for managing karst ecosystems in the context of carbon neutrality goals.

title: Elemental and isotope geochemistry of Smackover Formation brines in Alabama and Arkansas: Implications for fluid mixing and water-rock interaction
description: Publication date: Available online 11 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Kelly Kreitzer, Ming-Kuo Lee, Haibo Zou, Yang Wang, Andrew L. Masterson, Ann Sullivan Ojeda, Zeki, M. Billor, Natalia Malina, Gregory M. Guthrie, Bonnie McDevitt, Ann Arnold, Demi Durham
abstract: This study investigates the geochemical characteristics of brines within the Upper Jurassic Smackover Formation in Alabama and Arkansas through elemental and isotopic analyses and geochemical modeling to reveal the extent and nature of fluid mixing and water-rock interactions. Smackover Formation brines exhibit Na-Cl-Ca hydrogeochemical facies and sulfate depletion relative to seawater. Lower sulfate concentrations, coupled with high H2S concentrations in some brines (0-364 mg/L) at temperatures >80°C, suggest that thermochemical sulfate reduction occurred. Cl/Br and Na/Br ratios indicate that salinity was controlled by the mixing of meteoric water with evaporated seawater that had reached halite saturation, rather than by halite dissolution. The δ18O and δ2H values of the brines also suggest mixing between meteoric water and evaporated seawater that had reached gypsum and halite saturation. Geochemical modeling of seawater evaporation predicts a Cl-Na or Cl-Mg facies after halite saturation, contrasting with the observed Cl-Ca dominance of the Smackover Formation brines. The Ca-enriched brines may have evolved from Cl-Mg-dominated evaporated seawater through dolomitization of limestone. The 87Sr/86Sr ratios range from 0.70740 to 0.71048, higher than the average of Jurassic seawater (0.707). The non-linear relationship between 87Sr/86Sr and 1000/Sr suggests alteration of brine geochemistry by fluid mixing or by inputs from Sr and 87Sr-enriched rock sources. Lithium concentrations are positively correlated with 87Sr/86Sr ratios and TDS in brines enriched in these constituents. These correlations suggest deeper-seated geogenic sources and have implications for Li exploration in the northern Gulf Coast basin. Normal faults associated with the pre-Jurassic topography may have provided potential pathways for brine migration into the Smackover Formation under the influence of overpressure or thermohaline convection in the Gulf Coast.

title: A mineral-centric framework for predicting arsenic behaviour in lithium mine wastes
description: Publication date: Available online 3 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Quentin Bollaert, Quentin Dehaine, Fernando Prado Araujo, Sonja Lavikko, Hugh O’Brien, Olivier Mathon, Valérie Cappuyns
abstract: The expansion of lithium mining in Europe is essential for securing strategic raw materials, but it raises increasing challenges for long-term tailings management. Arsenic (As), present at trace levels in lithium ores, can partition into mine wastes during beneficiation, yet its mineral hosts and solid-phase speciation remain poorly constrained due to low concentrations and diffuse distribution. This limits predictions of arsenic behaviour during processing, leaching, and storage, while current assessments often rely on bulk data that overlook key mineralogical controls. Here, we combine quantitative mineral deportment with As K-edge XANES to characterise arsenic distribution and speciation in ores and residues from three major European lithium projects. Arsenic occurs across sulfide, sulfarsenide, silicate, oxide, and phosphate phases, typically at trace levels but within abundant minerals. Sulfarsenides are dominated by As(–I), whereas other phases show mixed speciation (As(–I), As(III), As(V)). Linear combination fitting indicates overall dominance of As(–I) and As(V), with As(III) minor and sample-specific. XANES of leaching residues reveal the oxidation of arsenic released during arsenopyrite dissolution to As(V), followed by its immobilisation under specific pH conditions, demonstrating that arsenic leaching behaviour at disposal sites is strongly controlled by weathering conditions. Coupled with traditional leaching approaches, this mineral-centric framework quantifies the contribution of As-bearing phases and their control on release across environments, supporting more targeted tailings management and improved environmental strategies for lithium production.

title: Lithology-dependent evolution of wettability and water adsorption during supercritical CO 2 -water-rock interactions: implications for caprock sealing efficiency and CO 2 plume migration
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Xuwei Hou, Jienan Pan, Xiaoqiang Wan, Pengzhou Tian, Xiaoyu Wang, Qinghe Niu
abstract: Deep coal seam-targeted carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) offer a technologically viable and high-impact pathway to abate anthropogenic CO2 emissions and steer the global transition toward carbon neutrality. The evolution of water adsorption and wettability within caprock seals exerts primary control on both the migration patterns of CO2 plumes and the long-term integrity of geological carbon storage. However, the mechanisms governing these changes, particularly the lithology-dependent responses of rocks to supercritical CO2 (ScCO2)-water-rock interactions, remain poorly understood. This study conducted time-dependent supercritical carbon dioxide-deionized water-rock interaction experiments on medium-grained sandstone and sandy mudstone caprock samples from deep coal-bearing strata under reservoir conditions (40 °C and 8 MPa). A combination of X-ray diffraction (XRD), contact angle measurements, inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), and dynamic volumetric sorption measurements (DVS) were used to systematically track the evolution of mineralogy, geochemistry, and surface properties over time. Water contact angles increased substantially during ScCO2-water-rock interactions. For medium-grained sandstone and sandy mudstone, the increases reached 212.63% and 385.71%, respectively, implying a transition in wettability from strongly hydrophilic toward near-neutral conditions. Calcium, potassium, and sodium showed similar depletion trends in both lithologies, whereas magnesium and iron exhibited contrasting trends, with relative enrichment in medium-grained sandstone and depletion in sandy mudstone. The moisture adsorption capacity exhibits distinct temporal evolution trends: medium-grained sandstone initially rises then falls during the early reaction stage, reaching its peak after 20 days; while sandy mudstone shows a continuous decline throughout the entire experimental period. The pseudo-first-order kinetic model can accurately reproduce the adsorption process of the two rock types with time. Correspondingly, after 30 days of reaction, the capillary breakthrough pressure decreased by 75–81%, indicating a significant decline in the sealing efficiency of the caprock. These findings elucidate the lithology-dependent mechanisms controlling wettability alteration and water adsorption evolution during ScCO2-deionized water-rock interactions and provide fundamental insights for evaluating CO2 plume migration, caprock integrity, and the long-term security of geological carbon storage in deep coal seams.

title: Dawsonite deposition and metal transport during natural carbon capture and storage in a geothermal system
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Paolo S. Garofalo, Farshid Kiani, Barbara Umfahrer, Francesco Dellisanti, Simone Beccari, Ivan Callegari, Daniele Rappuoli, Detlef Günther
abstract: Dawsonite is an AlNa carbonate that is documented in several geological environments. This mineral gained global attention due to its potential role in Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) via long-term mineral trapping, but its genesis in nature is incompletely constrained. In this work, we present a case of dawsonite mineralization that provides constraints on its genesis. The study area is the Mt. Amiata geothermal system (Italy), which hosts intense CO2 venting and an historical district of HgSb mineral deposits. Here dawsonite is long known to form within the cap rocks of the geothermal system. We combine remote sensing data, field mapping, microthermometry and Raman spectrometry of fluid inclusions, mass transfer calculations, elemental imaging by Laser Ablation-Inductively Coupled Plasma-Time of Flight Mass Spectrometry, CO isotopic compositions, and geochemical modeling to provide constraints into the process of dawsonite deposition. We show that at Mt. Amiata dawsonite deposition is extensive, fracture hosted, and is probably a product of chemical vapor deposition, i.e., mineral deposition from heterogeneous reactions involving a vapor phase. Dawsonite deposited from an effervescing H2O-NaCl-CO2 fluid at c. 100 °C, PCO2 ≥ 2 MPa, and aNa+/aH+ > 106 together with a group of transition metals (Ni, Co, Fe, Cr, Cu, Pb, Zn) and geothermal pathfinder elements (Hg, Sb, Ga, Tl, Ag), which occur as oxides or as trace elements in the host rock minerals. Dawsonite-bearing joints and veins are interpreted as escape structures of fracture-controlled, metal-bearing, low-T hydrothermal fluids in an area of intense CO2 venting of this geothermal system.

title: Two general mechanisms for scheelite formation in hydrothermal systems
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Xiangchong Liu, Wei Li, Karel Breiter, Hao Liu, Mihal Tarassov, Hui Wang, Yun Gao
abstract: The mechanisms that promote scheelite formation in hydrothermal systems remain incompletely understood, despite their fundamental importance for understanding the tungsten minerals in tungsten deposits worldwide. The Xingluokeng deposit (South China, ∼0.30 Mt. WO₃), characterized by the coexistence of abundant scheelite and wolframite within a granitic host, provides an ideal natural laboratory for addressing this question. Trace element analyses show that biotite contains an appreciable amount of tungsten (≤43 ppm W) compared to plagioclase (<1 ppm W), but did not contribute significantly to the W budget of scheelite; Instead, the W source was derived from magmatic-hydrothermal fluids or pre-existing tungsten minerals (e.g., wolframite). In contrast, biotite decomposition during chloritization and local disappearance adjacent to quartz veins released Fe and minor Mn, facilitating wolframite precipitation during early mineralization. Two distinct mechanisms promoted scheelite precipitation during progressive cooling and depressurization. The first is a Ca-driven mechanism, in which Ca influx produces scheelite alone. A two-end-member Sr isotope mixing model indicates that approximately two-thirds of the Ca influx came from granitic melts and Ca-rich plagioclase, with the remainder derived from more radiogenic Neoproterozoic sedimentary rocks. The second mechanism, identified here for the first time, is S-driven scheelite precipitation associated with ferrous sulfide. In-situ S isotope analyses of sulfides coexisting with scheelite yield δ34S values close to 0‰, consistent with a dominantly magmatic source. Thermodynamic calculations further show that the dominance of scheelite plus ferrous sulfides over wolframite is favored by declining temperature, near-neutral pH and elevated reduced S content. These results demonstrate that scheelite formation can be controlled not only by Ca addition but also by S-induced Fe2+ sequestration. Together, these mechanisms provide a unified framework for understanding scheelite precipitation across diverse environments, including carbonate-hosted tungsten deposits (e.g., skarn), and granitoid- and clastic sediment-hosted tungsten and gold deposits (e.g., orogenic).

title: Fe isotopes reveal a carbonate-bearing eclogitic source for the Shandong nephelinites
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Jin-Hua Shi, Gang Zeng, Li-Hui Chen, Xiao-Jun Wang, Jian Zhao, Hao-Yuan Yu
abstract: Recently, the genesis of Cenozoic intraplate mantle-derived rocks in eastern China (particularly nephelinites) is frequently linked to the deep cycling of surficial carbonate components. However, the source lithology of these rocks remains under debate, with carbonated peridotite (formed through metasomatism via carbonate-derived melt/fluid) and carbonate-bearing eclogite as two potential candidates. Here, high-precision Fe isotopes of these nephelinites are reported to constrain the source lithology. The δ57Fe values of these nephelinites (0.24–0.37‰) are significantly higher than those of MORB (0.16 ± 0.04‰). Quantitively modelling based on newly reported Fe–O force constants reveals that an oxidized peridotitic source is insufficient to produce melts with such elevated δ57Fe values. Furthermore, the trace element ratios of these nephelinites, characterized by high Zn/Fe, low Mn/Zn, and low Co/Fe, also indicate the lithology of their mantle source is non-peridotitic. Consequently, we propose that, in addition to mantle oxygen fugacity, the presence of eclogitic components in the source is a key factor contributing to the heavy Fe isotopic compositions of these mantle-derived magmas. On the one hand, the involvement of recycled crustal materials oxidizes the mantle, thereby imprinting the magma source with heavy Fe isotopic signatures. On the other hand, the partial melting of such non-peridotitic materials, namely carbonate-bearing eclogite, further intensifies Fe isotopic fractionation in the resultant magmas, a process that plays a particularly critical role in amplifying this isotopic effect. Thus, this study highlights that Fe isotopes can serve as an effective tracer for distinguishing carbonated peridotite from carbonate-bearing eclogite in the mantle. Our new constraint on the mantle source lithology of nephelinites from eastern China (i.e., carbonate-bearing eclogite) reveals the essential role of recycled crustal materials in generating the heavy Fe isotopic signatures of intraplate nephelinites, with broad implications for understanding deep carbon cycling and mantle dynamics.

title: Genesis of the Palaeoproterozoic banded iron formations (BIFs) in the Rangpur Saddle, Dinajpur, Bangladesh: Constraints from geochemistry, fluid inclusions and zircon U-Pb geochronology
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): A.S.M. Mehedi Hasan, Ismail Hossain, Shruti Rana, Kwan-Nang Pang, Toshiaki Tsunogae, Mark I. Pownceby, Jarred Lloyd, Mohammed Masum
abstract: In this research, for understanding the tectonogenesis in Hakimpur iron deposits with different rock types and geochronology, the data were obtained from petrography, XRF, ICP-MS, LA-ICP-MS, petrography and Raman spectroscopy of fluid inclusions. The deposits are characteristically high-grade Superior-type banded iron formation (BIF) that shows alternating light and dark bands, constituting chiefly of opaque minerals (i.e., magnetite, hematite and/or goethite) and quartz. LA-ICP-MS zircon U-Pb dating of a siderite-bearing quartzite, the associated rock to the BIF, indicates the depositional age of ∼1.74 Ga. The BIF bands are found in association with amphibolite, biotite schist, and quartzite. The concentration of Al2O3, TiO2 and ∑REE in BIFs (1.29 wt%, 0.08 wt% and 161.35 ppm, respectively) indicates they primarily originated from iron-rich chemical sediments, possibly influenced by the addition of terrestrial or volcanic materials. However, markedly low content of trace element compositions such as Cr, Ni, Co, V and Sc clearly indicates the incorporation of terrigenous sediments with passively volcanic materials. REE–Y signatures, Eu/Eu⁎ P AAS, Y/Ho, Eu/Sm and Sm/Yb ratios also suggest the BIFs formed through the precipitation (low-temperature) of hydrothermal fluids and seawater blend, accompanied by a notable detrital contribution. The basin in which they accumulated was characterized by restricted circulation and redox stratification, consistent with a localized ferruginous basin rather than direct Great Oxidation Event (GOE)-type conditions. δ18O and fluid inclusion reflect clay minerals were altered during diagenesis and metamorphism in the sediments as- clay (illite) → chlorite → biotite → amphibole. This occurred through hydrothermal action in subduction-related orogenic system during concurrent magmatism of Palaeoproterozoic basement along CITZ in Bangladesh.

title: Unraveling the enrichment mechanism of indium in sphalerite: Insights from causal machine learning and global geochemical data
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Xuan Zhao, Jing Xu, Shubing Ouyang, Taiping Zhao
abstract: Sphalerite serves as the primary host mineral for the critical metal indium, yet the mechanisms driving its extraordinary enrichment remain controversial. Specifically, the respective roles of source fertility and physicochemical conditions (e.g., temperature and redox states), as well as their synergistic enrichment mechanisms, remain unclear. Traditional linear statistical methods struggle to quantify these synergistic effects due to the complex nonlinear characteristics of geological data, while standard “black-box” machine learning models lack geological interpretability, making it difficult to effectively decouple the contributions of source characteristics and precipitation mechanisms. A comprehensive analytical framework integrating interpretable machine learning, the Kernel Conditional Independence (KCI) test, and Causal Forests was established to address these limitations. Using a global sphalerite dataset, key geochemical variables controlling In enrichment, along with their nonlinear thresholds, were quantitatively identified. The results indicate that: (1) The combination of Fe > ∼4 wt% and Mn > ∼4000 ppm constitutes a thermodynamic prerequisite, indicating high-temperature, reduced magmatic-hydrothermal environments favorable for In enrichment; (2) Synergistic interactions between Cu and Sn constitute the core driving mechanism; effective enrichment occurs when Cu > ∼120 ppm and Sn > ∼1 ppm. This threshold behavior reflects the synergistic control between Cu-mediated charge-balancing lattice substitution and magmatic source supply traced by Sn; (3) Conversely, Ge acts as an important constraint, with its enrichment corresponding to low-temperature, non-magmatic basinal brine systems (e.g., Mississippi Valley-type (MVT) deposits) unfavorable for mineralization. These findings demonstrate that exceptional In enrichment is not governed by a single factor but is jointly determined by InSn sources affinity, lattice substitutions, and specific high-temperature, reduced environments. This research provides a rigorous quantitative geochemical basis for assessing critical metal resources, bridging the gap from correlation identification to causal inference.

title: Sorption behavior and surface complexation modeling of Co(II) and Ni(II) on granite
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Yujia Zhang, Wenbo Zhang, Zechen Zhang, Qichen Yao, Zongyuan Chen, Qiang Jin, Zhijun Guo
abstract: 60Co and 63Ni are important activation products formed during the operation and decommissioning of nuclear facilities. Their retention and migration in host rocks are therefore important issues in the safety assessment of radioactive waste disposal. In this study, the sorption of Co(II) and Ni(II) on granite from the Beishan high-level radioactive waste preselection site in Gansu, China, was investigated using batch-type experiments under both single-sorbate and binary coexisting conditions. The experimental results show that Co(II) and Ni(II) sorption on Beishan granite is strongly affected by pH and ionic strength, and both ions exhibit similar sorption behavior. Electron probe microanalysis showed that Co and Ni were heterogeneously distributed on the rock surface and tended to accumulate on minerals rich in reactive sites, such as biotite and chlorite. To describe the sorption process quantitatively, a generalized composite (GC) model was developed. In this model, the intrinsic cation-exchange sites of granite were considered, while mineral surface hydroxyl groups were represented by equivalent SOH sites. Three sorption reactions were included, allowing the model to reproduce the Co(II) and Ni(II) sorption data obtained under different experimental conditions. The predicted proportions of surface species SOM+ and SOMOH (M = Co or Ni) at pH 8.5 by the proposed GC model were consistent with the XPS peak analysis, supporting the validity of the model. The model was further applied to granite from the Yangjiang low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste repository in Guangdong, China. With the reaction types and equilibrium constants fixed, the model reproduced the Co(II)/Ni(II) sorption data for Yangjiang granite after the site capacities were scaled to the specific surface area. These results suggest that the GC-based surface complexation model is applicable to granitic host rocks from different sites and can provide useful parameters for predicting the retention and migration of divalent activation products.

title: Geochemical distribution and mineralogical control of scandium in karst bauxite, NW Sardinia, Italy
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Alfredo Idini, Paola Mameli, Giovanni Mongelli, Emanuela Schingaro, Guido Cerri, Maria Lacalamita, Ernesto Mesto, Amid Ouladmansour, Matteo Luca Deidda, Stefano Naitza, Giacomo Oggiano
abstract: In the last years, karst bauxite have attracted considerable attention as secondary sources of critical metals, including scandium and, in this respect, we investigated the geochemical pathways of scandium in karst bauxites from the Nurra district, north-west Sardinia (Italy). The Nurra karst bauxite mainly consist of boehmite, goethite, hematite, kaolinite, and anatase. In the whole-rock the average Sc concentration is 51 mg/kg. Microanalysis show that Sc is, by far, hosted in Fe-rich domains where the average Sc content is 171 mg/kg. An unusual content of Zr is measured all along the micro analyses, dispersed ubiquitously in both Fe-rich domains and Al-rich domains. The distribution of Sc and Zr in neoformed structures, such as Fe–“agate” and Fe-veins, suggests that these elements were mobile during the formation of these textural components. The Nurra bauxite hosts three main zircon populations of different age that are disrupted, fractured and corroded. Only one zircon population has been identified as the main Sc host (from 1184 to 4164 Sc mg/kg). We suggest that the source of Sc in the Nurra bauxite comes from the partial dissolution of the Sc-rich zircon since: (i) no other Sc-bearing primary mineral has been detected; (ii) the UCC-like parent material and (iii) the Zr content dispersed in all the bauxite micro domains suggesting that Zr may experience a significant degree of mobility during bauxitization. On these basis, further studies are needed to investigate the pH oscillations during karst bauxite formation and their implications on the geochemical mobility of critical elements.

title: Experimental coefficients for the partitioning of Zn between dolomite and brine at 125 to 200° C
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Sarah E. Smith-Schmitz, Martin S. Appold, Hector M. Lamadrid
abstract: The concentration of Zn in aqueous fluids fundamentally affects the origin of sediment-hosted base metal ore deposits. Zinc concentration in ancient aqueous fluids can in principle be determined by direct measurement in fluid inclusions, from solubility theory, or by comparison to analogous modern fluids. However, attempts to employ these approaches are commonly hindered by uncertainties in how to interpret fluid inclusion analyses, uncertainties in the values of pH, redox potential, or sulfur concentration, or the compositional heterogeneity of modern crustal fluids. Partitioning theory provides a potential alternate way of determining Zn concentrations in aqueous fluids from measured Zn concentrations in a mineral that precipitated from that fluid, like dolomite, a common ore-stage mineral in sediment-hosted base metal deposits. The present study was undertaken to determine experimental partition coefficients (D) for the partitioning of Zn between water and dolomite under typical sediment-hosted base metal ore formation conditions. To this end, a series of dolomite precipitation experiments was performed at temperatures of 125, 150, 175, and 200 °C, pressures of 10 MPa and the saturation pressure of the aqueous solution, and Zn concentrations of 10, 100, and 1000 ppm for experimental durations of 10 to 80 days. Powder X-ray diffraction analysis of the resultant mineral precipitates indicates that they all consist predominantly of dolomite. Measured Zn/Mg ratios in the precipitates and the fluids were used to calculate D values of 42.1 ± 6.3, 30.5 ± 4.5, 20.7 ± 5.6, and 43.2 ± 9.2 at temperatures of 125, 150, 175, and 200 °C, respectively.

title: Variation of K-rich magma formation during early Aegean arc migration, NE Greece
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): J.P.M. Wolf, K.M. Haase, M. Regelous, J. Falkenberg, E.M. Hars, P. Voudouris
abstract: Magmatic activity in the Aegean region has migrated southward by ∼400 km over the past ∼34 Ma due to rollback of the subducting African plate, producing age-progressive magmatic centres. In NE Greece, its earliest stage is recorded in the Maronia Magmatic Corridor, where magmatism between ∼34 and 29 Ma evolved from calc-alkaline in the northeast to shoshonitic compositions in the southwest. We present new major-element, trace-element (n = 67), and Sr-Nd-Pb-isotope (n = 36) data for volcanic and plutonic rocks to investigate magma generation and evolution during early Aegean arc migration. The magmatic rocks define geochemically distinct calc-alkaline and shoshonitic suites. The most mafic samples (4–10 wt.% MgO) show higher (Ce/Yb)N ratios in the shoshonite suite (10.8 ± 2.0) than the older calc-alkaline suite (5.5 ± 1.1), accompanied by distinct mean 206Pb/204Pbi ratios (18.68 ± 0.04 vs. 18.78 ± 0.03). Both suites evolved along coherent fractional-crystallisation ± assimilation trends, although the shoshonitic magmas show mantle-source heterogeneity. Lavas with transitional compositions (206Pb/204Pbi: 18.73 ± 0.01) bridge the two suites. Volcanic and plutonic rocks within individual centres display geochemical similarities, indicating common parental magmas and interconnected plumbing systems. Elevated P₂O₅ contents in transitional (0.4 ± 0.1 wt.%) and shoshonitic (0.6 ± 0.2 wt.%) magmas reflect increasing contribution from phosphorus-rich shallow-marine sediments, distinct from the pelagic sediments dominating the older calc-alkaline magmas. Our results show that changes in subducted pelagic-to-shallow-marine sediment input during slab rollback control K-enrichment in early Aegean arc magma generation, offering a geochemical framework for identifying discrete slab compositional inputs in migrating arc systems.
