By integrating P sequential extraction, metagenomic sequencing and multivariate analyses, the influence of P fraction on microbial community succession was examined in these contrasting sedimentary environments. Results showed that distinct depth-dependent patterns emerged. Bacterial α-diversity decreased significantly with depth only in XXKL, while archaeal diversity exhibited a unimodal trend in DXKL. Deterministic processes dominated archaeal community assembly in DXKL, whereas stochastic processes, as inferred by the neutral community model, played a more important role in XXKL. Organic P fractions (HCl-Po or NaOH-Po) consistently emerged as the primary drivers of microbial diversity, with lake-specific shifts regulated by sediment pH: HCl-P prevailed in neutral-to-weakly alkaline DXKL, while NaOH-P dominated in weakly acidic XXKL. Structural equation modeling further revealed that organic matter and pH indirectly shaped community composition by modifying P bioavailability. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that P fraction composition fundamentally regulates microbial community assembly and vertical succession via its control over P fraction bioavailability. This study provides useful mechanistic understanding for P management and ecological restoration in large freshwater lakes facing eutrophication risks.

title: The influence of hydrophobic agent on unsaturated seepage mechanisms in silty clay: insights from electrical resistivity monitoring
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Jiayi Tian, Deliang Ma, Xiaoliang Yao, Teng Li, Tianyang Lan, Dongliang Ji, Huaiping Feng
abstract: Hydrophobic modification represents a promising approach to limiting water ingress into geotechnical structures. During water migration, soil hydrophobicity and water content interact dynamically, rendering barrier performance moisture dependent and difficult to characterize using conventional equilibrium based methods. To address this limitation, a soil column apparatus integrating multilevel electrical resistivity monitoring with the transient profile method was developed to continuously monitor water infiltration in hydrophobic soil and determine unsaturated hydraulic conductivity. One dimensional infiltration tests were conducted on silty clay specimens with n-octyltriethoxysilane (OTES) contents of 0–0.8%, and resistivity measurements were used to reconstruct volumetric water content profiles. The sequential resistivity responses at different height levels captured the upward propagation of the wetting front. Increasing OTES content delayed initiation onset, prolonged the time required to reach moisture equilibrium, reduced equilibrium volumetric water content, and increased spatial differences in water content along the soil column. OTES treatment reduced hydraulic conductivity by approximately one order of magnitude. A modified content-dependent Gardner (C-G) model was established by relating the Gardner parameters to OTES content. The proposed framework enables continuous, non-destructive monitoring of water migration and determination of unsaturated hydraulic conductivity in hydrophobic soils.

title: Climate change impacts on alpine springs in Austria: shifts in discharge seasonality and water availability
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Martin Masten, Magdalena Seelig, Simon Seelig, Matevž Vremec, Thomas Wagner, Maria Obwegs, Matthias Hausleber, Jutta Eybl, Gerfried Winkler
abstract: Spring water supplies about half of Austria’s drinking water demand and is the sole source in some regions. Climate change is rapidly altering hydrological conditions in the Alps, making projections of future spring discharge essential for sustainable water management. This study assesses climate change impacts on 70 alpine springs across the Austrian Alps, covering a wide range of climatic and hydrogeological settings. Plausible catchments were identified using a rainfall–runoff model with a snow module, which was forced with climate projections from three emission scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5) and 40 model realizations to evaluate impacts until 2100. Changes were assessed by comparing a historical reference period (1980–2009) with a near-future period (2030–2059) and a far-future period (2070–2099). Analyses were conducted for individual springs and hydrologically classified spring groups. Results indicate decreasing spring discharge in western Austria under all scenarios and periods. Under RCP 4.5 and 8.5, discharge reductions also emerge in southern Austria. Annual discharge changes generally remain within single-digit percentages, in both positive and negative directions, but differ among spring groups. Snow-dominated and recession-dominated springs show the highest sensitivity to emission scenarios, whereas fast-responding springs maintain positive annual changes. Seasonal shifts are pronounced, with increased spring time discharge for snow-dominated springs and reduced summer and autumn discharge for both snow-dominated and fast-responding springs. Low flows shift from late winter and early spring toward summer and autumn, intensifying under higher-emission scenarios. These results provide a basis for climate adaptation and sustainable water management in Austria.

title: Groundwater discharge dominates CO 2 emission with low CH 4 efflux in a glacier-fed stream on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Chuan Wang, Xin Dai, Sen Xu, Yueqing Xie, Yanxia Shen, Chunhui Lu, Wei Zhi
abstract: Glacier-fed streams are important yet poorly understood components of the cryospheric carbon cycle. It remains unclear whether these streams act as carbon sources or sinks, and what mechanisms drive carbon gas exchange. Here, we combined salt slug injection experiments, dissolved gas tracing (4He, 40Ar, 84Kr, O2, CO2, CH4), and 222Rn mass balance modeling to constrain CO2 and CH4 exchange in a glacier-fed stream on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Concurrent increases in stream discharge, electrical conductivity, stable water isotopes, and major ion concentrations indicated notable groundwater discharge. The 222Rn mass balance model revealed groundwater discharge rates per unit stream length of 3.2–43.1 m2 d−1 (∼34.7 % of increased stream discharge) and gas transfer velocities of 3.6–148.1 m d−1. The stream remained persistently oversaturated with CO2, whereas CH4 stayed near atmospheric equilibrium. Paired dissolved gas analysis indicated that in-stream metabolic CO2 production was limited (1.5–2.7 mmol m−2 d−1). In contrast, groundwater discharge supplied substantial CO2 inputs (11–2121 mmol m−2 d−1), sustaining oversaturation and driving rapid CO2 emissions (21.7–853.7 mmol m−2 d−1), which are comparable to or even higher than the global average for rivers. Groundwater CH4 inputs were small (0.1–21.5 μmol m−2 d−1), leading to low atmospheric exchange fluxes (−45.3 to 70.9 μmol m−2 d−1). Higher CH4 emissions occurred in reaches with elevated groundwater CH4 concentrations and high groundwater discharge rates. Our findings suggest that the glacier-fed stream can be a CO2 emission hotspot driven by groundwater discharge. We underscore that groundwater discharge, a fundamental yet underrepresented hydrological pathway, should be explicitly integrated into carbon cycling models for glacier-fed streams.

title: Mapping new pre-consolidation head, safe pumping buffer, and safe pumping volume for groundwater management in post-subsidence cities: a case study from Houston, Texas
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Guoquan Wang
abstract: The New Pre-Consolidation Head (NPCH), Safe Pumping Buffer (SPB), and Safe Pumping Volume (SPV) are critical thresholds for the safe use of groundwater resources without reactivating land subsidence in post-subsidence urban areas. NPCH refers to the hydraulic head in a confined aquifer system at the time subsidence ceased; as long as heads remain above this level, permanent subsidence will not resume. SPB represents the difference between the current hydraulic head and the NPCH, indicating the maximum permissible hydraulic head decline before subsidence is reactivated. SPV estimates the maximum volume of groundwater that can be safely extracted within the SPB limit. Although these concepts are well-established theoretically, their practical application is hindered by the complex temporal and spatial variability of hydraulic heads in thick confined aquifer systems, as well as limitations in field monitoring data such as the spatial density and temporal coverage of monitoring wells. This study demonstrates practical approaches for mapping NPCH, SPB, and SPV in Harris-Galveston Subsidence District (HGSD) of southeast Houston, Texas. The resulting maps reveal significant spatial variability in subsidence vulnerability and available safe reserves. Critically, the NASA-Clear Lake area—a densely populated high-technology hub hosting the NASA Johnson Space Center—retains only approximately 5 m of SPB as of 2025, implying that increased groundwater pumping in this area could promptly reinitiate unrecoverable subsidence. In contrast, the adjacent Pasadena area maintains a substantially larger SPB of 24 m, with a corresponding SPV sufficient to serve as an emergency water source for neighboring zones. As of 2025, the total SPV across HGSD Areas 1 and 2 is estimated at about 58 MGD (million gallons per day) on an annual basis, equivalent to roughly 1.5 times recent annual groundwater use. The mapping techniques for NPCH, SPB, and SPV presented here are adaptable and can be implemented in other urban areas where subsidence has ceased.

title: Anthropogenic dominance of water storage variability in the Yellow River Basin: A machine learning synthesis of multi-source data (1981–2031)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yanping Cao, Zunyi Xie, Dandan Liu, Chaolin Mu, Jielun Wang, Yihao Chang, Yingjun Pang
abstract: Water is critical to sustainable development in arid river basins such as the Yellow River Basin (YRB), where rapid population and economic growth have profoundly altered the hydrological regime. However, the historical evolution and future trajectories of water resources, together with the relative roles of natural and anthropogenic influences, remain incompletely understood, limiting effective water management and ecohydrological sustainability. Here, we integrated satellite observations, model simulations, and machine learning methods to reconstruct terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) from 1981 to 2002 and forecast monthly TWSA through 2031. Our results identify a pivotal transition around 2000, when TWSA variability in the YRB shifted from being predominantly associated with climatic fluctuations to being increasingly associated with human activities. This transition was accompanied by concurrent changes in climatic and ecohydrological conditions and increasing anthropogenic pressures. Before 2000, TWSA variations were primarily associated with natural hydroclimatic fluctuations and showed only a modest decline. After 2000, socioeconomic development and large-scale ecological restoration became increasing associated with accelerated TWSA depletion. More recently, depletion moderation alongside water-conservation initiatives and increasing precipitation, although no statistically significant hydrological turning point was detected. Across three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, residual non-climatic influences, which may include anthropogenic effects and processes not represented by the selected climatic predictors, accounted for approximately 84%–97% of the projected TWSA trends. This dominant residual contribution highlights the importance of non-climatic influences on future water storage trajectory in the basin. This study provides sustainable water management, policy, and adaptation in water-limited basins facing growing supply–demand imbalances.

title: Groundwater data assimilation under prior misspecification: A comparative study of state-of-the-art methods
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yuxin Ye, Jiangjiang Zhang, Lei Yao
abstract: Data assimilation (DA) is a key tool for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification in groundwater modeling. For high-dimensional groundwater DA problems, the ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ESMDA), the iterative local updating ensemble smoother (ILUES), and the deep-learning-based ensemble smoother (ES(DL)) can be employed under different problem settings and assumptions. These methods are commonly formulated within a Bayesian framework, in which performance depends strongly on the proper specification of prior information, observation operators, and error statistics. In practice, however, prior misspecification is often unavoidable because of incorrect assumptions about parameter ranges, spatial structures, and probability distributions, yet its impact on groundwater DA performance remains poorly understood. Here, this study presents a systematic evaluation of groundwater DA under diverse prior misspecification scenarios. Specifically, this study considers a challenging joint inversion problem involving eight contaminant source parameters and a 3321-dimensional heterogeneous hydraulic conductivity field, constrained by limited and weakly informative observations of hydraulic head and contaminant concentration. The performances of ESMDA, ILUES, and ES(DL) are examined under various types of prior misspecification. The results show that prior misspecification can degrade assimilation performance for all three methods, while their relative robustness depends on the inversion target, evaluation metric, and the type and severity of prior misspecification. These findings highlight both the critical role of prior misspecification in groundwater DA and the importance of selecting appropriate DA methods based on specific inversion objectives and prior conditions.

title: Rainfall selectivity in large dry heatwave events across the contiguous United States
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yajie Shi, Wei Dai, Xiangrui Xu, Yuyou Zhi, Xi Zhang, Yinglong Chen, Weijun Fu
abstract: Large dry heatwave events are generally treated as rainfall-suppressed extremes, yet whether rainfall can still emerge within these dry-hot envelopes, and under what controls, remains unclear. Here we analyse 821 large summer dry heatwave events across the contiguous United States during 1950–2024 using an event-based Lagrangian framework that tracks retained heatwave envelopes, rainfall propagation and local candidate-front realization. Rainfall was not uniformly excluded from these events. Instead, rainfall realization was spatially reorganized: at the main threshold of ≥ 1 mm d–1, the United States-mean trend was weak (−0.13 percentage points per decade), but this masked a much stronger eastern increase (+1.09 percentage points per decade). Larger heatwave envelopes also did not translate into proportional rainfall occupation: event-scale area coupling between heatwave and rainfall extent weakened from r = 0.64 at ≥ 1 mm d–1 to r = 0.33 at ≥ 5 mm d–1, while zero-rain events increased from 49 to 357. Heatwave geometry constrained rainfall propagation more strongly in distance than in direction, with displacement coupling remaining positive but weakening from r = 0.79 to r = 0.59 as rainfall intensity increased. At the local front scale, realized rainfall cells were preferentially selected towards stronger humidity, moisture convergence and instability support, and four-variable discrimination skill increased from an AUC of about 0.74 at ≥ 1 mm d–1 to about 0.84 at ≥ 5 mm d–1. These results show that large dry heatwaves are not uniformly rain-free hazards, but spatially selective hydroclimatic structures in which rainfall can still be realized where atmospheric moisture, convergence and instability provide local support within an otherwise dry-hot envelope.

title: Coastal aquifer vulnerability to salinization under sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction pressure in a Mediterranean karst system
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): R. Álvarez Alonso, P.A. Robledo Ardila, C.A. Melo Aguilar, J.J. Durán Valsero, R. Morales, S. Martínez Pérez
abstract: Sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction are reshaping coastal systems in karst environments, particularly in low-gradient coastal plains where groundwater-dependent ecosystems are strongly coupled to aquifer dynamics. However, most coastal assessments remain based on topographic inundation and shoreline retreat, neglecting groundwater processes that influence the inland propagation of marine influence. This study presents a GIS-based hydro-coastal vulnerability screening framework designed to identify areas potentially influenced by the combined effects of sea-level rise and groundwater stress. The approach integrates (i) DEM-based potential marine inundation, (ii) hydrogeological signals of piezometric decline and salinization derived from monitoring data, and (iii) a multi-criteria hydro-coastal vulnerability index incorporating ecological sensitivity, hydrogeological susceptibility, anthropogenic pressure, and system resilience. Direct potential marine inundation alone affects between 9.24 and 43.76 km2 (0.25–1.20% of the island) across sea level rise scenarios but underestimates the inland extent of coastal influence. Including groundwater indicators identifies a broader scenario-based coastal influence zone and increases ecosystem exposure, with up to 97% of wetland area potentially exposed within the integrated coastal-influence zone under high-end scenarios. Vulnerability is concentrated in low-lying coastal plains, particularly in s’Albufera, Campos–Es Trenc, and Albufereta, where strong aquifer–sea connectivity and anthropogenic pressure converge. These findings suggest that coastal evolution in Mediterranean karst settings emerges from the interaction between surface and groundwater processes and highlight that hydrogeologically informed regional screening approaches may identify coastal areas extending beyond static representations of the MTPD, thereby informing future coastal-domain management rather than redefining regulatory boundaries.

title: Reconstructing terrestrial water storage and quantifying drought evolution in Australia using LSTM networks
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Bo Feng, Yan Xu, Nan Jiang, Biaobiao Guo, Peng Yin, Ao Guo, Tianhe Xu, Harald Schuh
abstract: High-precision monitoring of Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) is critical amid climate-driven increases in drought severity. To overcome the inherent limitations of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE)—coarse spatial resolution and data gaps and the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)—uneven station distribution and high-frequency noise, we introduce a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework. This framework reconstructs high-quality TWS across Australia by integrating Equivalent Water Height (EWH) time series, meteorological data, and temporal markers to effectively capture GNSS-GRACE discrepancies. Joint inversion results demonstrate substantial spatiotemporal consistency with Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS), GRACE, and precipitation records. Notably, the LSTM-enhanced EWH significantly improves agreement with benchmarks: the correlation with GRACE reached 0.854 in the Northern Territory and surged from 0.290 to 0.656 in station-sparse Western Australia. Crucially, the model successfully bridges the GRACE mission gap, ensuring TWS continuity. Furthermore, the quantification of drought evolution (2011–2023) using a derived Drought Severity Index (LSTM-DSI) and NscPDSI revealed a correlation of 0.663, demonstrating robust consistency in capturing extreme hydrological signals. By integrating the temporal resolution of GNSS with the physical stability of GRACE, this multi-source fusion approach provides a robust foundation for investigating hydroclimatic interactions in Australia.

title: Recent intensification of the negative physiological effect of CO 2 on terrestrial evaporation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Haiyang Qian, Weiguang Wang, Zefeng Chen, Akash Koppa, Guoshuai Liu, Jian Zeng, Jianyu Fu, Shuai Cheng, Diego G. Miralles
abstract: Atmospheric carbon dioxide (aCO2) directly modulates global terrestrial evaporation (ET) through two counteracting plant physiological effects: vegetation greening and a reduction in stomatal conductance. The extent to which these two aCO2 physiological effects translate into ET trends, and their individual contributions, are still subjects of debate. Here we present a novel analog framework to decouple and quantify their respective contributions using a suitable global dynamic vegetation model ensemble from the TRENDY project, rigorously constrained by satellite observations. Our analysis, enabled by isolating the aCO2 physiological effect, reveals that the net physiological effect of CO2 on ET is globally negative during 1982–2018, as stomatal conductance reductions overcome the positive effect of greening. However, in water-limited arid regions, the decoupled effect shows a near-zero positive response. As aCO2 has increased in recent decades, this net negative physiological effect on ET has progressively intensified and is expected to attenuate the projected increases in ET due to global warming and the consequent acceleration of the water cycle.

title: Integration of vertical and lateral erosion in modelling landslide mass flows, debris flows and flash floods
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Ruochen Jiang, Wenjun Lu, Shihao Xiao, Xin He, Ruiqiang Bai, Yingyue Han, Mingdong Wei, Dalei Peng, Jian He, Limin Zhang
abstract: Overtopping and lateral erosion play a critical role in geomorphological evolution due to landslides, debris flows, fluvial floods and dam-breaching floods. These processes contribute substantial materials to runoff channels, significantly amplifying the flow volume and destructive power. Existing physics-based models suffer from oversimplified flow dynamics (e.g., constant flow properties or 1D approaches that ignore lateral erosion) or high computational costs (e.g., full 3D fluid dynamics simulations), limiting their accuracy and applications. To address these limitations, this study presents a novel depth-averaged numerical framework that simultaneously captures overtopping and lateral erosion dynamics. Beyond simulating these key erosional mechanisms, the model uniquely incorporates dynamic feedback between erosion processes and evolving properties of the flowing mass. The model performance is demonstrated through rigorous validation across three benchmark cases: (1) controlled dam-breaching experiments, (2) the 2020 Zelunglung landslide-debris flow cascade, and (3) the 2018 Sedongpu outburst flood. The simulations closely match measured topographic changes, confirming the framework ability to capture coupled erosion dynamics. The proposed model offers a useful tool for assessing large-scale cascading hazards and their geomorphic impacts, bridging the gap between computational efficiency and physical reality.

title: Optimal reservoir flood-control operation under successive rainfall events during the Meiyu season
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yuchang Mo, Yunfei Li, Shuaisen Ma, Qingan Qiu, Rui Peng
abstract: Reservoir flood-control operation during the Meiyu season is challenged by successive rainfall events, compound flood-wave superposition, and the conflicting objectives of flood safety and operational economy. Existing studies often represent rainfall uncertainty through independent events or aggregated inflow scenarios, which may overlook the temporal clustering and self-exciting characteristics of successive Meiyu rainfall events. This work develops a dynamic staged spillway-operation framework for reservoir flood-control scheduling under clustered rainfall conditions. A marked Hawkes process is employed to characterize the stochastic occurrence and temporal dependence of successive rainfall events, while a duration-corrected Gamma response kernel is introduced to describe the runoff generation and superposition process. Based on these components, a threshold-driven scheduling model is established, in which spillway operation levels are adaptively adjusted according to the real-time conditional non-failure probability. The optimal threshold structure is obtained by minimizing the expected operating cost through a nested Monte Carlo simulation framework coupled with particle swarm optimization. A case study of the Xin’anjiang Reservoir demonstrates that the proposed framework provides a better balance between flood-control reliability and operational cost compared with empirical, conservative, and aggressive scheduling strategies. Further analyses reveal that rainfall clustering characteristics, runoff-response parameters, and initial reservoir storage conditions significantly influence the optimal operation strategy. The proposed framework offers a risk-responsive and cost-aware approach for reservoir flood-control operation under successive rainfall events during the Meiyu season.

title: Improving predictions of annual nutrient and sediment loads across the Southeast United States with refined SPARROW model parameters
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Anjali Kumari, Ebrahim Ahmadisharaf, Victor Roland, Sumon Hossain Rabby
abstract: Limited research has focused on predicting nutrients and sediments across large regions. The SPAtially Referenced Regression on Watershed attributes (SPARROW) is a primary example of a regional water quality model for the Contiguous United States. In some regional versions of the model, such as the Southeast SPARROW model, urban land cover is the only explicit land cover source term, limiting its ability to fully account for underlying nutrient and sediment processes. Here, we refined the Southeast model (1.6 million km2) by introducing cropland, pasture, forest and wetland as explicit diffuse source and delivery terms, coupling land cover with Soller surficial geology classifications to represent geology-dependent sediment generation and re-estimating land-to-water delivery and in-stream transport/decay parameters. The refined model (RSPARROW) was calibrated against estimated mean annual loads of total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP) and suspended sediment (SS) at ∼600 monitoring stations across the Southeast United States. Compared to the baseline model, the refined RSPARROW improved Kling–Gupta efficiency by up to 21% for TP (0.58–0.70), with predictive uncertainty reduced by up to 31.5% for SS. Improvements were generally greater at smaller spatial scales, in catchments with milder slopes and in homogeneous, low-relief ecoregions in terms of all water quality parameters; the relationship between ground slope and model performance was stronger at larger spatial scales. The refined model can be used to more accurately predict annual loads and yields of nutrients and sediment across the Southeast United States and support coordinated water quality management among agencies charged with pollution control.

title: Global assessment of river flow regimes simulated by reach-level streamflow datasets
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Qiuyu Luo, Xiaomang Liu, Kaiwen Wang, Peng Bai, Zelong Yang, Ye Jing, Changming Liu
abstract: Global river flow regimes reflect riverine environmental conditions and are essential for sustaining natural ecosystems and human socio-economic systems. Recent advances in reach-level streamflow datasets have enabled spatiotemporally continuous representation of river flow, more closely reflecting real-world river networks than previous coarse grid-scale approximations. Assessment of these reach-level datasets is a prerequisite for their broad application, yet, existing assessments predominantly focus on their agreement with daily observations, overlooking their ability to capture multi-dimensional flow regime characteristics. Here, we assessed the performance of three reach-level datasets, namely the Global Reach-Level Flood Reanalysis (GRFR), the Global River Discharge Reanalysis (GRDR), and the Global Daily Reach‐Level River Discharge Data Set Based on Grid LSTM‐RAPID (GRADES-hydroDL). Using these datasets, we derived 38 streamflow indices across five flow regime dimensions (i.e., streamflow magnitude, frequency, duration, timing, and variability) and evaluated them against observations from 4,698 hydrological stations worldwide via different statistical methods. Using the Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) across streamflow indices, we find that GRADES-hydroDL outperforms the other datasets but remains limited in capturing low-flow magnitude and in frequency and duration characteristics (KGE as low as − 0.11). Further decomposition of KGE into its three components reveals that performance loss can be largely attributed to temporal correlation and mean flow bias. Additional analyses of intermittent rivers show that all datasets consistently underestimate hydrological intermittency, although GRDR performs comparatively better. These findings provide guidance for selecting reach-level datasets based on their performance across different flow regime dimensions.

title: Optimal layout of LID facilities at an urban basin scale in piedmont cities: Case study of Jinan City, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yanjun Zhao, Jun Xia, Zongxue Xu, Lei Cheng, Gang Zhao, Xiang Zhang
abstract: Urban flooding has become an urgent issue for cities around the world, endangering human life and property. Piedmont cities have a special topography and complicated overland flow processes, thus creating challenges for the spatial optimization of LID facilities. We developed an urban hydrological model by coupling the TVGM-USWM and SWMM-LID module, considering various LID facilities and flow routing in urban drainage systems. We applied this model to the Huangtaiqiao drainage basin in Jinan City, which is one of China’s first pilots for sponge city construction. The NSGA-II algorithm was combined with the urban hydrological model to investigate the most cost-effective flood reduction scheme of LID facilities under different design rainfall processes. Results showed that: (1) The five LID facilities provided by the model were effective in reducing runoff volume and peak flow, thus demonstrating the model’s applicability; (2) There was a non-linear correlation between flood reduction rate and economic costs, with the cost-effectiveness of LID facilities decreasing when the design rainfall return period increased; and (3) PP and RB generated better economic returns in both RV and RP . LIDs in the PSA were more cost-effective under different design rainfall events, particularly GR in RP . Moreover, the study can provide LID layout schemes that either maximize flood reduction for a given economic cost, or minimize the economic cost for a given level of flood reduction. The findings of this study could provide the scientific decision-making for LID spatial layouts at the urban basin scale in piedmont cities.

title: Large-scale climate teleconnections and multiscale controls on river water temperature
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Hadi Sanikhani, Mostafa Khorsandi, Stephen J. Déry, André St-Hilaire
abstract: River water temperature dynamics are influenced by climate variability and large-scale atmospheric teleconnections, particularly in regulated river systems where anthropogenic controls interact with natural hydroclimatic drivers. This study investigates the multiscale influence of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) on river water temperature variability in a cold-region Pacific watershed influenced by Pacific climate variability. Long-term daily water temperature series were reconstructed for 1950–2024 using the hybrid Air2Stream model, and the resulting series were analyzed over the common 1950–2021 period using wavelet techniques, including the continuous wavelet transform and bivariate, partial, and multiple wavelet coherence. Results indicate that while seasonal atmospheric forcing dominates the annual thermal cycle, significant non-stationary variability emerges at interannual (2–7 years) and decadal scales. The PDO exhibits persistent and coherent coupling with river water temperature over multi-year to decadal timescales, whereas ENSO influences are episodic and primarily confined to interannual timescales. Joint PDO-ENSO interactions are most pronounced at decadal (8–16 year) periods. Comparison between regulated and natural stations suggests that flow regulation may differentially filter low-frequency variability, reducing raw interannual-to-decadal power while partially preserving coherent phase relationships with basin-scale climate modes in regulated reaches. Summer-focused analyses reveal that positive PDO phases are consistently associated with elevated river water temperatures, with mean July-September (JAS) anomalies of approximately 0.2–0.8 °C and increased exceedance frequencies above ecologically relevant thresholds (e.g., 20 °C). In contrast, ENSO-related summer temperature anomalies are weaker and spatially inconsistent. Overall, the results demonstrate that decadal-scale Pacific climate variability, particularly the PDO, plays a persistently influential role in shaping river water temperature variability in cold-region systems, highlighting the importance of accounting for non-stationary climate controls in hydrological thermal assessments.

title: A comprehensive distributed hydrological framework for assessing flood responses to environmental change under multiple human disturbances
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Yuhao Wang, Ke Zhang, Edwark Park, Yuning Luo, Jie Liu, Shunzhang Li, Zhaoan Zhang, Yue Kong, Sheng Wang
abstract: Understanding flood responses to environmental change and simulating flood processes under multiple human disturbances are essential for reliable prediction under a changing environment. To address these challenges, this study enhances the GHydroMod-SIM-DAI model to develop a comprehensive distributed hydrological framework that explicitly represents human disturbances, including groundwater exploitation, hydraulic structure operation, land cover change and on-farm water storage. An improved underground reservoir module is introduced to capture the effects of water table decline on runoff generation in mountainous watersheds, while a field ridge interception module is incorporated to quantify surface flow interception by agricultural ridges. The proposed framework is applied to five representative watersheds in the Haihe River Basin. During the baseline period (1980–1991), it demonstrates improved performance across all watersheds, with the best results in the Zijingguan Basin, followed by the Fuping, Songxi River, Qingshui River, and Shili River basins. Peak flow analysis indicates substantial attenuation due to human disturbances, with the largest reductions in the Qingshui River Basin (93.0%), followed by the Songxi River (59.9%), Zijingguan (42.5%), Shili River (41.3%), and Fuping (39.1%) basins. Afforestation, water table decline, and field ridge interception are identified as the dominant mechanisms driving peak flow reduction in different watersheds. During the change period (2006–2019), the enhanced underground reservoir module markedly improves performance in mountainous watersheds including the Shili River, Zijingguan, and Songxi River basins, while field ridge interception dominates peak flow reduction in the Qingshui River Basin, with a mean contribution exceeding 95% across the ten flood events. Although predictive uncertainty increases under a changing environment, the framework maintains satisfactory accuracy for moderate and major floods. Overall, this study provides a robust, process-based tool for quantifying flood responses to environmental change under multiple human disturbances in rapidly evolving watersheds.

title: Regional variability and driving mechanisms of runoff coefficient on the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Qilin He, Peng Zhang, Binbin Li, Nan Shen, Mingyi Yang, Dongli She, Fengbao Zhang
abstract: The runoff coefficient (RC), defined as the proportion of precipitation converted into surface runoff during an individual rainfall event, exhibits pronounced spatial variability across different geomorphic regions owing to the combined influences of climate, topography, vegetation, and human activities. Using the Loess Plateau as a representative study area, we integrated multi-site observations and conducted a cross-regional comparative analysis to quantify the regional variability of event-based RC and identify its driving mechanisms. The results showed that the hilly–gully region (HG) showed the highest mean RC (0.14), followed by the earth–rock mountain (RM, 0.11), whereas the sandy zone (SD, 0.08), gully region (GR, 0.07), and valley plain (VP, 0.06) exhibited considerably lower values. RC showed a distinct land use gradient, with bare land > cropland > orchard > forest > shrub > grassland. Under Light, Moderate, and Heavy Rain, HG showed the highest RC, whereas RM exhibited the highest RC under Storm Rain. Structural equation modeling identified rainfall characteristics and land use as the dominant drivers of RC. Rainfall exerted positive total effects on RC in RM (0.41), GR (0.36), HG (0.31), and SD (0.29), but a slightly negative total effect in VP (−0.08). Land use exerted positive total effects on RC, particularly in RM, VP, and SD (0.42, 0.36, and 0.49, respectively), whereas vegetation exerted negative total effects (−0.37, −0.22, and −0.19, respectively). Soil moisture and terrain generally exerted weaker total effects on RC, with total effects varying markedly among regions. Overall, these results provide new insights into the regional variability and controlling mechanisms of RC across the Loess Plateau, supporting region-specific soil and water conservation strategies.

title: Mechanistic characterization of the discrepancies in enrichment of nitrate between agricultural and urban-industrial rivers in the semi-arid areas of northern China: Insights from multi-element stable isotope analysis
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Ang Dong, Yu Liu, Guiqi Liu, Guangzhi Rong, Shuaihao Liu, Mingjun Mo, Haixia Wang, Guoguang Wang
abstract: Numerous studies have investigated nitrate sources and transformations in surface waters, yet the mechanisms sustaining winter nitrate maxima in semi-arid rivers, where hydrological constraints limit external inputs, remain poorly understood. This study investigated the seasonal dynamics, driving mechanisms, and biogeochemical fate of nitrate in the agricultural and urban-industrial rivers of the semi-arid areas via the analysis of multi-element stable isotopes (δ 15N-NO3 -, δ 18O-NO3 -, δD-H2O and δ 18O-H2O). Nitrate concentrations showed seasonal discrepancies in both rivers, with high concentrations in winter. Principal component analysis implied that monsoon-driven hydrological dilution was the main factor controlling the seasonal variability of nitrate in the two rivers. Partial least squares path modelling revealed divergent winter enrichment mechanisms: in the agricultural river, water-column nitrification (59.56 ± 26.47%) and benthic nitrate release (40.44 ± 26.47%) jointly contributed; in the urban-industrial river, physically driven benthic release dominated. Fractionation-corrected Bayesian mixing modelling confirmed that the nitrate was primarily derived from the chemical fertiliser and soil organic nitrogen in the agricultural river, while fertiliser and sewage dominated the non-urban and urban reaches of the urban-industrial river, respectively. However, winter apportionment results likely reflected legacy nitrogen historically accumulated in the sediment pool rather than contemporaneous external inputs. By contrasting agricultural and urban-industrial catchments, this study demonstrates that urban-industrial development has fundamentally reshaped nitrogen migration and transformation pathways in semi-arid rivers, providing a scientific basis for differentiated nitrate management strategies tailored to catchment-specific land-use conditions.

title: Where are the retention hotspots of microplastic particles in the riverbed with complex topography
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Haiyu Yuan, Guangqiu Jin, Kaiwen Zhang, Xue Ping, Ran Ma, Guiqiao Wang, Xiangfei Qi, Hanqing Zhao
abstract: Riverbeds are critical microplastic (MP) sinks, yet the spatial heterogeneity of retention within three-dimensional complex topographies remains poorly understood. This study developed a coupled surface water-groundwater model, combined with laboratory-derived filtration properties, to investigate the spatiotemporal accumulation and retention hotspots of MPs. Results demonstrate that MP infiltration is governed by the competition between intrinsic settling/rising velocities and topography-induced interfacial fluxes across diverse polymer types. While small MPs act as near-passive tracers following hyporheic streamlines, larger MPs are dominated by gravitational settling, with over 95% of the input mass retained within 5 days. Spatiotemporal mapping identifies high-intensity hotspots primarily on the lee faces of bedforms and near reattachment zones. Vertically, retention mass exhibits an increase from the crest followed by a power-law decline, with maximum accumulation occurring near the trough elevation and reaching depths of up to 9 cm. Crucially, 3D morphological features, such as saddles and lobes, create distinct longitudinal filtration strips that significantly diverge from idealized 2D predictions. This extreme spatial heterogeneity implies that MP stocks estimated from single sediment cores may contain substantial errors depending on the sampling position relative to riverbed topography. This research provides a mechanistic framework for identifying MP hotspots in natural rivers, highlighting the critical role of bedform morphology in shaping the long-term distribution of MP pollution legacies.

title: Evaluation of Sobol’ sensitivity indices conditioned on model performance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Rishitha Bikkumalla, Rao S. Govindaraju
abstract: Hydrological modeling studies rely on global sensitivity analysis to determine parametric importance and to support calibration. In this regard, Saltelli’s Matrices Method (SMM) is widely used to construct Sobol’ sensitivity indices that quantify the fraction of output variance explained by individual parameters and their interactions. Sensitivity estimates depend not only on the objective function used to evaluate goodness of fit (e.g., NSE, KGE, RMSE), but also on the choice of a performance measure (e.g., NSE > 0.7) that determines which parameter combinations are deemed acceptable. However, filtering samples to retain only those that satisfy a performance criterion violates the paired matrix structure required by SMM, and no prior study has proposed a principled way to address this structural violation while preserving SMM’s efficiency. To resolve this gap, the Constrained Saltelli Matrix Method (CSMM) is proposed in this study. CSMM is a two-step filtering procedure that first retains samples satisfying a performance threshold in the first step and then reorganizes them into the design matrices amenable to SMM in the second step, yielding an “acceptable” subset on which Sobol’ indices can be estimated within a performance-constrained parameter space. The second filtering step distorts the input parameter distribution relative to the threshold-filtered space, and the Hellinger distance is proposed as a practical diagnostic to quantify this distortion and assess the reliability of the resulting sensitivity indices. CSMM is applied to the HEC-HMS rainfall-runoff model for twelve events across three watersheds in the Midwestern USA, with Time of Concentration ( T c ) and Storage Coefficient ( R ) treated as uncertain parameters. Sensitivity estimates from CSMM are compared against a brute-force binning method applied to both threshold-filtered and acceptable samples. CSMM estimates are found to be in good agreement with the binning results when the Hellinger distance is small, and to diverge as distortion increases, supporting the use of the Hellinger distance as a guide to CSMM’s applicability. The results further show that parameter sensitivities shift as the performance threshold becomes more stringent, with a T c – R trade-off emerging under NSE-based conditioning, while R dominates under KGE and peak-flow-based conditioning. These findings underscore that variance-based parameter sensitivity is linked to both the modeling objective and the level of acceptable performance, and that CSMM provides a principled means of conducting Sobol’ sensitivity analysis conditional on satisfactory model performance.

title: Differences in watershed hydrochemical evolution driven by anthropogenic disturbances and geological heterogeneity: from source apportionment to hydrological process response
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Qi Long, Hui Qian, Yicheng Duan, Kang Li, Yanyan Gao, Yixin Liu, Siqi Li, Xiaoxin Shi, Zhiming Cao, Qiaoyang Yang
abstract: Quantitatively resolving surface water and groundwater sources and clarifying how surface water-groundwater interactions (SGI) control hydrochemical evolution under anthropogenic disturbances and heterogeneous geological environments are crucial for watershed management. This study selected the Lao River and Feng River basins in the Guanzhong Basin, characterized by distinctly different geological features, as study areas. By employing hydrochemical and isotopic analyses combined with the Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) and Bayesian isotope mixing (MixSIAR) models, we systematically investigated hydrochemical evolution processes and SGI characteristics under varying geological backgrounds and human activities. The results reveal pollution patterns and hydrological processes driven by geological heterogeneity and human activities. Both rivers are primarily controlled by natural weathering. However, the Lao River is profoundly influenced by agricultural activities, whereas the Feng River receives relatively minor agricultural impact. Although both rivers exhibit similar spatial SGI patterns, notable differences emerge in their second reaches. The Feng River, characterized by fine-grained sediments and clay interlayers, maintains perennial runoff primarily through upstream surface water recharge (73.5%). Conversely, the widespread distribution of coarse-grained aquifers with strong vertical connectivity in the Lao River basin leads to river drying, with groundwater recharge to surface water accounting for 48.3%, presenting a higher estimated contribution compared to that of the Feng River (18.6%). The contrasting SGI patterns generate distinct environmental risks. In the Lao River, groundwater discharging into surface water may elevate nitrate concentrations, threatening water quality, while the Feng River faces rapid pollutant migration and potential urbanization impacts. These findings emphasize the necessity for differentiated watershed management strategies. Ultimately, this study establishes an integrated framework combining chemical source apportionment with SGI analysis, demonstrating the efficacy of comprehensive hydrochemical and isotopic approaches in uncovering geochemical processes under complex environmental conditions.

title: The iFLUX sensor for real-time measurement of horizontal groundwater flux magnitude and direction
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Niels Van Putte, Goedele Verreydt
abstract: Groundwater management requires reliable insights into subsurface water flux, yet effective long-term remote flux monitoring remains technically challenging due to power requirements, the difficulty of detecting low flux magnitudes, and the high operational on-site effort required by some methods. Here, we present the iFLUX horizontal flux sensor, which measures groundwater flux magnitude and direction in real time by using two perpendicularly oriented microfluidic flow chips, representing the first in situ hydrogeological application of this technology. The sensor is designed for use in fully saturated, non-cohesive porous media and is installed within a dedicated prepack filter. The complete system is deployed in a borehole drilled specifically for this purpose to ensure controlled and reproducible installation depth and orientation of the sensor. We evaluated the sensor’s magnitude and directional accuracy and assessed the stability of the measurements in a controlled laboratory sand tank experiment. Furthermore, we calibrated the sensor for flow-field distortion across a range of hydraulic conductivities using numerical modelling. Within the imposed range of 1 – 35 cm/day Darcy flux, the measured flux magnitude followed the imposed flux with an RMSE of 1.15 cm/day and an R2 of 0.99, while directional accuracy was 4.55° (RMSE). A sensitivity analysis indicated that sensor-based flux measurements are less sensitive to uncertainty in hydraulic conductivity than Darcy-based flux calculations, where flux errors scale linearly with hydraulic conductivity errors. Overall, the sensor’s low power demand, fast response and sensitivity for low flux magnitudes suggest potential for long-term autonomous monitoring of groundwater flux in low-gradient and dynamic environments.

title: Vegetation change reshapes meteorological-hydrological drought characteristics and propagation process in the Yellow River Basin, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part C Author(s): Xiaoyang Li, Jun Xia, Beibei Hu, Xuanxuan Wang, Lingling Bin, Xilong Wang, Juan Zhang, Guangpeng Wang
abstract: Current large-scale global vegetation restoration has profoundly altered the terrestrial water cycle, but its feedback regulation on drought evolution warrants deeper investigation. Taking the Yellow River Basin (YRB) from 2001 to 2024 as a case study, this research employed a distributed hydrological model incorporating vegetation dynamics (DTVGM-PT-JPL) to derive meteorological (SPEI) and hydrological drought indices (SRI) from simulation results under changing and constant vegetation scenarios, thereby linking vegetation with drought and evaluating how vegetation change in YRB regulated drought characteristics and propagation processes. Results showed that meteorological and hydrological droughts across YRB generally weakened during the study period due to the warming-wetting climate tendency in upstream regions, while scenario comparison indicated that the characteristics of both drought types exhibited asymmetric sensitivity to vegetation change. In the middle reaches where vegetation restoration was significant, the frequency, duration, and intensity of hydrological drought increased beyond the extent of meteorological drought. The propagation process from meteorological to hydrological drought also exhibited spatial heterogeneity, with shorter propagation times and higher probabilities in the middle and lower reaches, while the upper reaches showed the opposite patterns. Compared to the vegetation constant scenario, the vegetation change scenario exhibited a shorter drought propagation time within the basin and exerted a nonlinear amplifying effect on drought propagation across different severity levels. The vegetation change driven by restoration in YRB primarily raised the probability and thresholds for meteorological drought to trigger mild and moderate hydrological droughts under the adopted scenario framework, but this enhancement gradually weakened as hydrological drought severity increased. These research findings can provide scientific reference for synergistic management of ecological restoration and drought risk at the basin scale.

title: Modelling a decade of daily open water evaporation for existing and planned water storages: A spatially explicit analysis for the Pilbara region of north-western Australia
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): David L. McJannet, Stephen B. Stewart, Dejun Cai, Thomas G. Van Niel, Tim R. McVicar, Steven D. Boxall
abstract: We present a method that integrates physically based evaporation modelling approaches with high-resolution meteorological data interpolated from land-based observations to estimate daily open water evaporation at local and regional scales across the data-sparse Pilbara region of north-western Australia. The evaporation modelling approach considers water body heat storage and enables water bodies of different sizes, depth and salinity to be modelled. Daily meteorological data were interpolated at 0.01° resolution for the 440,000 km2 Pilbara region based on the best performing model from up to 14 thin plate spline models per meteorological variable, which used varying combinations of latitude and longitude, elevation and a coastal distance index as spatial predictors. Using the interpolated meteorological data, the evaporation model was run across the study region (at a daily time step with 0.01° spatial resolution) for all combinations of water body size and salinity. Comparison of model results with measurements for three different sized water bodies yielded R2 > 0.64 and an RMSE of < 1.6 mm d−1 giving confidence in results. Reference water body evaporation was high across the focus area and ranged between 2272 and 2965 mm y−1. We showed that the spatio-temporal open water evaporation model can be used to estimate evaporation for both existing and proposed water bodies. To simplify model application to different waterbody characteristics we developed an evaporation scaling factor which was used to scale model results from a reference water body (surface area of 1 km2, salinity of 10 mS cm−1 and depth of 10 m) to any water body with surface area between 0.01 and 5 km2 and salinity between 0 and 300 mS cm−1. The method developed provides the first daily-scale open water evaporation estimates across the Pilbara region and can be applied to other locations where open water evaporation estimates are required for water resource management by using spatially interpolated meteorological grids and/or reanalysis products.

title: Groundwater-mediated divergence in forest soil CO 2 emissions under extreme rainfall: hydrological and microbial perspectives at watershed scale
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Pengtao Wang, Bairui He, Huihui Han, Jun Zhang, Fei Yu, Xin Wang, Yidi Wang, Shaoqing Liu
abstract: Increasingly frequent extreme rainfall events are altering carbon availability for forest soil microbes, introducing substantial uncertainty in soil CO2 emissions. This study investigated the dynamics and underlying mechanisms of forest soil CO2 emissions in the Qi River Basin (QRB), a temperate forest watershed frequently affected by extreme rainfall. Using a combination of hydrological modeling, simulated rainfall experiments, and field investigations, we found that groundwater flow is the dominant control on both autotrophic and heterotrophic respiration rates, explaining 46.6% of their variability. From 2001 to 2020, total forest soil CO2 emissions − derived from soil microbial respiration rates (Rmicrobe) and root respiration rates (Rroot) – showed distinct two-stage interannual variations, with an annual mean of 285.0–305.0 g C m−2 yr−1. Laboratory and field experiments indicated that extreme rainfall suppressed Rmicrobe primarily through the loss of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) via surface runoff, which depleted bioavailable carbon for soil microbes. In contrast, Rroot increased as reduced groundwater flow might indirectly influence root exudation. We observed significant differences (P < 0.05) in both DOC concentration and composition in surface runoff between upland forests and the downstream river; Microbial abundances also differed significantly (P < 0.05) between these sites. Groundwater flow, rather than surface runoff, was identified as the primary driver of spatial variability in both DOC and microbial abundance. Though annual forest soil CO2 emissions have stabilized recently, a projected decline in groundwater flow is expected to stimulate soil CO2 emissions. Targeted watershed management strategies focusing on maintaining groundwater recharge may be effective in enhancing temperate forest carbon sequestration and further confirmation is needed. These findings also highlight the role of subsurface hydrology in shaping forest carbon dynamics under changing rainfall regimes, with broader implications for improving the hydrological-carbon coupling in current Earth System models.

title: New insights into lacustrine groundwater discharge within the groundwater-wetland-lake system in arid regions
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Xinming Song, Fu Liao, Guangcai Wang, Xiaodong Li, Nuan Yang, Liang Guo, Luoyao Xiong, Chenyu Wang, Hanxiao Wang
abstract: Wetland-groundwater-lake interactions play a critical role in regulating water availability, hydrochemical evolution, and ecosystem services in arid regions. Wetlands commonly develop along lakes shorelines in arid regions, yet their regulatory role in lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) has received little attention. Here, LGD passes through wetlands and then entering the lake is defined as wetland-lake groundwater discharge (WLGD). We developed a novel method based on evaporation line (EL) slope variations, integrating with stable isotopes (δ18O and δ2H), 222Rn, and hydrochemical data, to identify WLGD in Hurleg Lake, Qaidam Basin. The observed lake water EL slope (4.89) is significantly lower than the value theoretically derived from river and precipitation inputs alone (5.18), indicating additional inflows characterized by strong evaporative signatures. Unlike direct LGD, WLGD is characterized by elevated TDS, enriched δ18O, and reduced 222Rn activity in lake water. Along the eastern shoreline, the progressive increase in TDS and δ18O enrichment, accompanied by decreasing 222Rn activities, further indicated the influence of wetland-derived groundwater inputs. These observations also validate the evaporation line slope as an effective tracer for identifying lake recharge sources. Furthermore, WLGD also substantially alters lake hydrochemistry by increasing pH, HCO3 –, NO3 –, and SO4 2- concentrations while decreasing ORP and water temperature. The findings provide new insights into the mechanisms and ecological significance of lacustrine groundwater discharge within integrated groundwater-wetland-lake systems.

title: Reactive transport processes in unsaturated porous media: inclusion of capillary geochemistry
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Shao-Jie Wu, Andrey P. Jivkov, Majid Sedighi
abstract: Reactive transport in unsaturated porous media is governed by coupled hydro-geochemical processes, where capillary water exists under negative pressure. Conventional reactive transport models assume that geochemical reactions in such systems behave identically to those in bulk water, i.e., they neglect the thermodynamic effects of capillary conditions. Porewater in unsaturated media, however, is often in a stretched state, which alters its thermodynamic properties and influences the mineral-water-gas interactions. Developed in this work is a hydro-geochemical reactive transport model that explicitly incorporates capillary geochemistry by extending the thermodynamic description of water, aqueous species, gases, and minerals into the negative pressure domain. The formulation is based on classical thermodynamics and implemented in OpenFOAM within a coupled multiphase flow and transport framework. The model is verified against thermodynamic databases and validated using laboratory-scale experiments and is further applied to field-scale CO2 injection. The results show that capillary influences geochemical behaviour primarily through pressure-dependent changes in molar volumes, which modify reaction Gibbs free energy and shift equilibrium constants. In contrast, the impact on activity coefficients is comparatively minor. Simulations demonstrate that stretched porewater enhances CO2 dissolution, promotes mineral reactions, and alters the evolution of porosity and permeability in unsaturated regions. At the field scale, these effects lead to enhanced near-well mineral precipitation, with implications for injectivity. Neglecting capillary geochemistry can therefore result in systematic errors in predicting reactive transport processes in geological CO2 storage systems. The work provides a physically consistent framework for linking capillary-dependent geochemistry with continuum theory in unsaturated porous media and highlights the importance of accounting for capillary geochemistry in geoenvironmental applications.

title: Synergy between lacustrine groundwater discharge and dissolved organic matter in regulating seasonal CH 4 and CO 2 emissions in an ice–covered lake–groundwater system
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yuanzhen Zhao, Lijuan Hu, Shen Qu, Heyang Sun, Chengcheng Xia, Chao Gu, Xu Yang, Zhongli Wang, Limin Duan, Xiaomin Liu, Ruihong Yu
abstract: Lakes in cold regions that experience seasonal ice cover are potential hotspots of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. However, the synergistic roles of groundwater, as a concealed external source, and dissolved organic matter (DOM) in regulating CH4 and CO2 dynamics and emissions remain poorly understood. Based on year–round observations at Ulansuhai Lake, this study revealed seasonal differences in the regulatory effects of lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) and microbially derived DOM. During the ice–free period, the LGD rate was low (5.53 mm/d). CO2 dynamics were primarily controlled by microbial decomposition of DOM, whereas CH4 dynamics were mainly influenced by direct LGD input and were positively correlated with DOM aromaticity and humification. During the ice–covered period, the LGD rate increased markedly, reaching a maximum of 18.09 mm/d, and became the sole external source of CO2. In contrast, CH4 was predominantly regulated by DOM, driven positively by humic component C2 and the humification index (HIX), a process facilitated by anaerobic microbial fermentation. Flux calculations indicated that, during the ice–free period, water–air emissions of both gases exceeded the corresponding LGD–derived inputs. However, when considering only the LGD pathway, its regulatory effect was stronger for CH4 than for CO2. During ice cover, water–air gas exchange ceased, while LGD–derived CO2 inputs (0.049–1.720 mmol/m2/d), together with CH4 produced via DOM–driven anaerobic fermentation, sustained greenhouse gas accumulation beneath the ice. These findings identify LGD as a concealed driver of CH4 and CO2 emissions with seasonal shifting roles and highlight its importance in carbon budget assessments of seasonally ice–covered lakes in cold regions. This study advances understanding of groundwater–derived carbon inputs in lake carbon cycling and provides both hydrological and biogeochemical insights for compiling greenhouse gas emission inventories from seasonally ice–covered lakes.

title: Connectivity and function determine whether ponds act as sources or sinks of nonpoint-source phosphorus
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Xiaofen Bai, Chen Lin, Ke Song, Wenlan Feng, Junfeng Xiong, Siyu Ge, Wanqian Yu, Jianchun Chen, Yijun Tong
abstract: Ponds can act as either sources or sinks for phosphorus (P) export within a watershed. However, most existing studies treat ponds as homogeneous units, lacking a quantitative framework to identify these opposing functions. To address this, we develop a source–sink diagnostic framework that couples index of connectivity (IC) for the pond–river network with P export simulated by an optimized SWAT+ model to identify P-source and sink ponds. Using the Taihu Lake Basin as a representative eutrophic watershed, the results indicate that: (1) Ponds play a small but critical role in P export. Although ponds account for only 0.78% of the watershed area, they contribute 22.76% of P export. (2) Correlations between IC and P export differ markedly across pond functional types. IC positively correlates with P export from aquaculture ponds (r = 0.74, p < 0.05) but negatively with landscape ponds (r = -0.75, p < 0.05); (3) An operational connectivity boundary at IC = − 2 helped distinguish source and sink zones: above this threshold, ponds predominantly act as P sources, dominated by strongly connected aquaculture ponds and moderately connected natural ponds. Below it, ponds shift to P sinks, mainly weakly connected natural and landscape ponds. This new framework provides the first quantitative basis for differentiated pond management, prioritizing source control in strongly connected aquaculture ponds while conserving sink functions in weakly connected natural and landscape ponds.

title: A synergetic framework for land-atmosphere coupling-based remote sensing inversion of evapotranspiration, surface resistance, and aerodynamic resistance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Xiaowei Wang, Yazhen Jiang, Huanyu Zhang, Yitao Li, Menglin Si, Yunsheng Lou, Zhao-Liang Li
abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key link in land–atmosphere interactions, governing the coupled exchange of water and energy. However, conventional remote sensing-based ET estimation methods generally parameterize aerodynamic resistance (rae ) and surface resistance (rs ) independently, which may limit the representation of their interplay and overlook the scale mismatch between them. To address this limitation, we propose a remote sensing-based ET coupling estimation framework (hereafter referred to as the ETC framework). Grounded in the intrinsic physics of surface energy balance, the ETC framework enables the simultaneous estimation of global ET, rae , and rs , with the land–atmosphere coupling coefficient (Ω) clarifying their coupling relationships. The reliability of the inverted resistance parameters was evaluated at 195 globally distributed flux sites. The inverted rs agrees well with PM-derived values, with an R2 of 0.56 and an RMSE of 73.86 s/m. Sensible heat flux estimated based on the inverted rae shows strong agreement with observations, with an R2 of 0.84 and an RMSE of 42.57 W/m2. The proposed ETC framework also demonstrates high accuracy in ET estimation: (1) at the half-hour scale, the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and R2 for ET estimates are 26.52 W/m2, 42.86 W/m2, and 0.88, respectively. The ETC framework also consistently outperforms the conventional PM baseline in reproducing measured ET; (2) at the monthly scale, ETC achieves higher accuracy than ERA5-Land, GLEAM, and TerraClimate products; (3) at the spatial scale, the global ET estimates show strong consistency with the three ET products. Consequently, by overcoming the critical limitations associated with independently parameterized resistances and neglected scale mismatches in conventional ET retrieval, the ETC framework enables the first synergetic, accurate estimation of ET, rae , and rs under physically constrained conditions across site-to-global scales. This achievement is expected to significantly advance the quantification of ET and the resistances.

title: Generating a consistent long-term L-band soil moisture record through Bayesian merging of SMOS and SMAP data
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Aoxing Zhao, Zushuai Wei, Linjie Guan, Beibei Yang, Jianxin Zhang, Bingsong Zhang, Tianjie Zhao, Lingkui Meng
abstract: L-band passive microwave remote sensing provides an indispensable tool for large-scale, long-term soil moisture monitoring. However, systematic biases arising from divergent sensor configurations, observational strategies, and retrieval algorithms across satellite missions—notably SMOS and SMAP—constrain the synergistic use of these vital datasets. Furthermore, the limited spatiotemporal sampling of any single satellite impedes applications requiring dense observational coverage. To address these challenges, this study establishes the SMAP soil moisture product as a reference dataset and develops a Bayesian framework to harmonize the SMOS record. Our methodology integrates SMOS L-band brightness temperature with MERRA-2 soil temperature data to generate a SMAP-consistent, long-term soil moisture dataset (SMOS_Reg) spanning 2010–2024. Validation analyses reveal good agreement between the corrected SMOS_Reg product and the SMAP reference at a global scale (2015–2022), with an ubRMSE of 0.033 m3/m3, a CC of 0.769, and a Bias of −0.002 m3/m3. Independent validation against ISMN ground measurements further confirms that SMOS_Reg achieves an accuracy (ubRMSE = 0.053 m3/m3, CC = 0.662) on par with the SMAP product (ubRMSE = 0.055 m3/m3, CC = 0.695), notably with a lower bias (0.013 m3/m3 vs. 0.028 m3/m3). Leveraging the orbital synergies between SMOS and SMAP, we developed a merged SMAP-SMOS_Reg product that significantly improves observational frequency, increasing the mean annual number of effective observation days by 61. This dataset may provide valuable support for future long-term applications in climate research, hydrological modeling, and drought assessment.

title: A network-based framework for deciphering extreme precipitation propagation across China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yingying Xu, Zhiyong Liu, Yifan Huang, Yuhao Liu, Caihong Hu
abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation under climate change pose growing challenges for disaster management and water governance. A network-based framework is developed that integrates spatial pattern analysis, propagation networks, community structures, and temporal evolution to characterize extreme precipitation propagation across China. Extreme precipitation events are robustly identified using a dual-threshold approach that accounts for regional characteristics and seasonal anomalies. A spatially constrained community detection method, combining the Louvain algorithm with K-means correction, is employed to delineate extreme precipitation propagation communities across eleven consecutive 5-year windows. Results reveal a pronounced southeast-northwest precipitation gradient, with coastal monsoon regions and the middle-lower Yangtze Basin acting as core propagation hubs, while arid inland and high-altitude regions remain weakly connected. Geomorphological features, including river valleys and mountain passes, serve as key relay corridors, facilitating long-distance signal propagation. Approximately 68% of propagation events occur within communities, with boundaries aligned to terrain and river basins while exhibiting clear nonstationary evolution over time. By capturing cross-basin propagation and trends of intensified propagation with shorter time lags, the analysis reveals how localized extremes are dynamically linked to system-scale cascading processes. The framework further provides a quantitative basis for diagnosing regional hydroclimatic connectivity, enhancing early-warning capabilities, and supporting coordinated cross-basin flood risk management in complex monsoon-influenced regions.

title: Constraining the maximum entropy production approach with sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence to estimate evapotranspiration in a seasonally dry deciduous forest
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): L.A. Méndez-Barroso, H.A. Gutiérrez-Jurado, G. Juárez-Cansdales, E.A. Yépez
abstract: Estimating evapotranspiration (ET) in arid and semi-arid ecosystems is crucial for understanding vegetation strategies to optimally use water storage in the vadose zone at different phenological stages. Currently, there are a limited number of ET techniques applicable to these ecosystems, especially to those found in remote and isolated areas, and able to partition and estimate soil evaporation (E) and plant transpiration (T). However, the development of simple thermodynamic models has allowed the estimation of energy balance components in both the soil and vegetation canopy, resulting in a better understanding of the seasonal variability of evapotranspiration. In this study, the maximum entropy production (MEP) approach was implemented and its performance evaluated in a semi-arid ecosystem (dry deciduous forest) to estimate the seasonal evolution of total evapotranspiration and canopy transpiration fluxes. In order to improve transpiration fluxes during the growing season, the MEP model was constrained with vegetation phenology at the site using remote sensing estimates of sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). Daily ET computed with the MEP approach performed very well (R = 0.96 and MAE = 0.32 mmd−1) in comparison with in-situ ET observations using the eddy covariance technique. Furthermore, MEP model showed an excellent robustness in transpiration estimates in comparison with independent state of the art-global transpiration assessments such as GLEAM (R = 0.84 and MAE = 0.87 mmd−1) and PML (R = 0.94 and MAE = 0.74 mmd−1). The thermal properties-based MEP approach is a reliable alternative for estimating evapotranspiration at long-term semiarid and remote monitoring sites because it uses simple meteorological observations as model input, unlike other approaches such as eddy covariance technique which implies costly equipment and significant investment of human and financial resources.

title: Economic impacts of saltwater intrusion on the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area under climate change scenarios
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yilin Chen, Zhihao Xu, Qian Dong, Zhifeng Yang
abstract: Saltwater intrusion is a global issue that impedes the development of coastal regions and poses risks to water supplies, particularly in areas such as the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA). While its drivers are well studied, the long-term economic effects under climate change scenarios, particularly indirect economic losses incurred by supply-chain effects, remain insufficiently explored. This study combines XGBoost and a Multi-Regional Input and Output (MRIO) model to assess the direct and indirect economic impacts of saltwater intrusion in the GBA. Salinity near eight river outlets was projected from 2025 to 2100 under SSP126, SSP370 and SSP585 scenarios. Direct economic losses were estimated based on salinity exceedance days and water supply dependence, while indirect economic losses transmitted through supply chains were quantified using the MRIO model. The results revealed that total direct economic losses ranged from 64.40 to 138.68 billion USD across SSP scenarios, while total indirect economic losses propagated through supply chains ranged from 47.44 to 101.52 billion USD. Jiangmen and Guangzhou emerged as the major source cities of indirect economic losses owing to their strong dependence on estuarine water supplies and extensive economic linkages. In cities such as Foshan, indirect losses exceeded direct losses by 78.42%–201.01%, highlighting the importance of supply-chain effects. Moreover, economic losses were not directly proportional to the severity of saltwater intrusion, indicating that the impacts were jointly influenced by salinity exceedance, water-supply dependency, and supply chains. These findings highlight the importance of integrating water resource management and economic resilience planning to mitigate the long-term impacts of saltwater intrusion under climate change.

title: A copula-based stochastic simulation method for the penman wind function (PWF) in in-stream evaporation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Minwoo Park, Ghani Rahman, Joo-Heon Lee, Hyun-Han Kwon
abstract: Accurately estimating in-stream evaporation is crucial for understanding surface water losses, but it remains challenging due to the sparse availability of flux data and the complex dynamics of flowing systems. This study introduces a modeling framework that combines the Penman Wind Function (PWF) with empirical-prior-based stochastic simulation to quantify uncertainty in in-stream evaporation estimates under data-limited conditions. Rather than demonstrating universal transferability of PWF coefficients, this study focuses on identifying how coefficient uncertainty and cross-site transfer bias emerge when reservoir-, stream-, and literature-derived parameters are applied across hydrologically distinct environments. Direct calibration of PWF coefficients using high-resolution flux data from the Andong Stream Experiment Center produced the most reliable estimates ( r = 0.862 , C o E = 0.731 , R M S E = 1.500 m m / d a y ), confirming that site-specific calibration remains the preferred option when local observations are available. To support applications where such observations are unavailable, we constructed a literature-derived empirical prior parameter library of PWF coefficients and used log-space Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) with copula-based Monte Carlo sampling to propagate parameter uncertainty. The literature-derived coefficient pairs were treated as a heterogeneous empirical prior library rather than as homogeneous i.i.d. samples.
